What Is a Timeshare? Why Financial Experts Say Avoid Them

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1893 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Choosefi

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.
  • A timeshare is a shared ownership or usage right in a vacation property.
  • The timeshare industry generates over $10 billion in annual sales, and roughly 9.9 million U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

A timeshare is a shared ownership or usage right in a vacation property. You pay an upfront purchase price — typically $20,000 to $40,000 — plus annual maintenance fees that at the moment average $1,120 per year and increase 3-5% annually. In exchange, you get the right to use a resort unit for a specific period each year, usually one week.

The timeshare industry generates over $10 billion in annual sales, and roughly 9.9 million U.S. households own at least one timeshare. But ownership satisfaction varies dramatically, and the financial reality rarely matches the sales presentation delivered during high-pressure resort tours.

Industry observers note that deeded (Fixed Week): You own a fractional interest in a specific unit during a specific week each year. This is actual real property — you receive a deed, it's recorded with the county, and you can theoretically sell, rent, or bequeath it. The problem: the secondary market for these deeds values most of them at near zero.

In a recent development, right-to-Use (Leased): You purchase the right to use a property for a set number of years (typically 20-40 years) but don't own real estate. At the end of the term, your usage right expires with nothing to show for it. This is common with newer resort brands.

In a recent development, points-Based Systems: Instead of a fixed week at a fixed resort, you purchase an annual allotment of points that can be redeemed at various properties within a resort network. Flexibility is the selling point, but availability at popular destinations during peak seasons is often limited — and points can inflate over time, requiring more points for the same week.

Timeshare companies spend an average of $4,000 in marketing costs per sale — and much of that goes toward the high-pressure sales presentations that are a signature of the industry. These presentations use urgency tactics ("this price is only available today"), comparison anchoring (showing the cost per vacation day), and emotional triggers ("don't you want the best for your family?"). The FI community's rule: never make a five-figure financial decision on the same day you learn about it. Walk away, run the numbers at home, and compare alternatives. The offer will still be available tomorrow — despite what the salesperson claims.

Timeshare sales presentations focus on the purchase price and the "cost per vacation night." What they don't emphasize is the total lifetime cost, which includes mandatory annual fees that increase every year, special assessments for major repairs, exchange fees if you want to trade your week, and the opportunity cost of that capital.

Let's run the real numbers on a typical timeshare over 20 years:.

At $4,204 per week over 20 years — without accounting for the opportunity cost of the capital — you can book luxury vacation rentals in most destinations for less money with zero long-term commitment.

Sources indicate that this is the most notable financial fact about timeshares: they have almost no resale value. The American Resort Development Association (ARDA) — the timeshare industry's own trade group — acknowledges that resale prices are a fraction of the original purchase price. In practice, most timeshares on the secondary market are listed for $1 or even offered for free, because the buyer inherits the mandatory annual maintenance fees.

Websites like RedWeek, TUG (Timeshare People Group), and eBay are filled with timeshare listings at $0-$1. Owners often can't give them away because the ongoing fee obligation makes them a liability, not an asset. This is the fundamental difference between a timeshare and a real investment: real investments appreciate or generate income. Timeshares depreciate to zero and generate mandatory ongoing costs.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

If you already own a timeshare and want out, here are your realistic options:.

Rescission Period: Most states give you 3-15 days after purchase to cancel without penalty. This is your best exit — if you're within this window, cancel immediately in writing via certified mail.

Recent findings suggest that sell on the Resale Market: List on TUG (Timeshare Users Group), RedWeek, or eBay. Set your expectations: you'll likely sell for $0-$1, and the "sale" is really about transferring the maintenance fee obligation to a willing buyer.

Contact the Resort's Deed-Back Program: Some major resort chains (Wyndham, Marriott, Hilton) offer deed-back or surrender programs where you can return the timeshare to the resort. Eligibility varies and there may be fees, but this is a legitimate exit path.

It has been revealed that timeshare Exit Companies: Proceed with Extreme Caution. The timeshare exit industry is plagued with scams. Legitimate exit attorneys exist, but many "exit companies" charge $3,000-$10,000 upfront and deliver nothing. The FTC and state attorneys general have pursued multiple timeshare exit companies for fraud. Before hiring anyone, check their BBB rating, look for complaints with your state attorney general, and never pay the full fee upfront.

The FI community has consistently found that travel rewards credit cards, vacation rental platforms, and strategic booking provide better vacation value than timeshare ownership:.

Here's the number that should end the timeshare debate for any FI-focused person: the average timeshare's annual maintenance fee ($1,120) invested in index funds at a 10% average return grows to $72,000+ in 20 years and $203,000+ in 30 years. Add the opportunity cost of the $24,140 purchase price invested instead, and the 30-year FI impact exceeds $440,000. That's nearly half a million dollars diverted from your FI number for one week of vacation per year at a resort you didn't choose.

Travel well, spend less, keep your FI timeline intact.

Choose a card that matches your spending patterns and offers flexible points or transferable miles. Sign-up bonuses alone often cover 1-2 free flights or hotel stays in the first year.

Sources indicate that pro tip: Pay the balance in full every month. Travel rewards only work financially if you never carry a balance and pay interest.

In a recent development, instead of paying $1,120/year in mandatory timeshare fees, deposit that same amount monthly ($93/month) into a high-yield savings account earmarked for travel. You'll have $1,120+ per year to spend on any vacation, anywhere.

In a recent development, research destinations on Airbnb, VRBO, and Booking.com. Booking 3-6 months ahead gets the best selection. Compare total costs including cleaning fees and service charges to timeshare equivalent costs.

Recent findings suggest that shifting your vacation by 2-4 weeks outside peak season saves 30-50% on flights and accommodation. Shoulder season often has better weather than peak season with fewer crowds.

If you were considering a $24,000 timeshare purchase, invest that money instead. At 10% average returns, $24,000 grows to $62,000 in 10 years and $161,000 in 20 years — all while you vacation on your own terms.

Pro tip: Set up automatic monthly investments for the amount you would have spent on timeshare financing payments.

A timeshare's purchase price ($24,140) plus 30 years of maintenance fees ($1,120/year growing at 3.5%) totals over $83,000 in direct costs. Invested in index funds at 10% average returns instead, that same money grows to over $440,000. That's the true cost of a timeshare — not the sticker price, but nearly half a million dollars of lost wealth-building potential over a career.

Recent findings suggest that no. A timeshare is a prepaid vacation blueprint, not an investment. Timeshares depreciate to near-zero resale value, generate mandatory ongoing costs that increase annually, and cannot produce income for the owner in most cases. The timeshare industry itself has moved away from calling them investments because of regulatory scrutiny.

The average annual maintenance fee is $1,120, according to ARDA (the industry trade group). Fees increase an average of 3-5% per year and are mandatory — you must pay them whether or not you use your timeshare. Some resort areas (Hawaii, ski towns) charge $1,500-$2,500+ per year. Special assessments for major repairs can add $1,000-$5,000 in any given year.

Industry observers note that technically yes, but practically it's very difficult. The secondary market is flooded with inventory at $0-$1 prices because most owners are trying to escape their maintenance fee obligations. Resale companies that promise to sell your timeshare for thousands of dollars are almost always scams. The most realistic options are deed-back to the resort, transfer to a willing buyer at $0-$1, or working with a licensed timeshare exit attorney.

The resort will send your account to collections, report the delinquency to credit bureaus (damaging your credit score), and potentially pursue legal action. For deeded timeshares, the resort can foreclose on the property. Maintenance fee obligations are contractual and legally enforceable — you cannot simply walk away without consequences.

Sources indicate that some are, many are not. The FTC has pursued multiple timeshare exit companies for fraud. Red flags include: demanding full payment ($3,000-$10,000) upfront, guaranteeing results, using high-pressure sales tactics similar to timeshare presentations, and lack of BBB accreditation. If you need exit help, consult a licensed real estate attorney in the state where the timeshare is located.

It has been revealed that in very narrow circumstances: if you genuinely vacation at the same resort every year, the annual cost (maintenance fees amortized with purchase price) is lower than booking that same unit independently, and you purchased on the resale market for $0-$1 (avoiding the $24,000+ retail markup). Even then, you're locked into one destination with escalating fees. For most people, the flexibility and cost advantage of alternatives makes timeshares a poor choice.

Recent findings suggest that A timeshare is a prepaid vacation plan with a near-zero resale value, mandatory escalating fees, and an extremely difficult exit process. The average timeshare costs over $84,000 across 20 years of ownership — and that money invested instead could grow to over $440,000 in 30 years. Modern alternatives like travel rewards cards, vacation rentals, and strategic off-peak booking deliver comparable or better vacation experiences with zero long-term commitment. If you're building toward financial independence, a timeshare is one of the most damaging financial products you can buy. If you already own one, explore deed-back programs or resale as your fastest path out.

One Bike for Everything? Our Editors Tested Hybrid Bikes for Daily Riding—These 10 Picks Are Best for Commuting, Fitness, and Light Trails

📅 23 Jul 2018 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2335 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • When I worked in bike shops, we sold tons of hybrid bikes.
  • According to recent reports, outside of cycling circles, the term “hybrid” often refers to vehicles that pair an electric motor with an internal combustion engine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

When I worked in bike shops, we sold tons of hybrid bikes. These bicycles are ideal for riders who say, “I need a bike that does a little of everything.” If you’re seeking versatility, a hybrid is often your best bike option. They’re a good choice for general fitness, commuting, running errands, and family rides.

According to recent reports, outside of cycling circles, the term “hybrid” often refers to vehicles that pair an electric motor with an internal combustion engine. However, in bike-speak, hybrids are a bicycle style that combines elements of road bikes and mountain bikes. Hybrids range from lightweight, sporty bikes designed for roads and bike paths to more rugged models suitable for light off-road use.

While they’re not ideal for die-hard mountain bikers or roadies seeking speed and the highest performance, hybrids work surprisingly well for many people on real-world rides. Typically, hybrids blend the lightweight frame, fast-rolling tires, and larger gears of road bikes with flat handlebars and the upright riding position of hardtail mountain bikes. Some hybrid models also feature suspension forks similar to those used on bikes designed for more aggressive, technical trails.

In a recent development, the Cannondale Quick 3 is our overall favorite hybrid for its fast feel and smooth ride, comfortable upright riding position, and reasonable price. These qualities make it great for new riders who may be hesitant about incorporating regular bike riding into their routine.

The Quick 3 features a comfortable Selle Royal saddle and Ergon grips. It also has mounts for adding a rear rack (the fork lacks rack mounts, however) and fenders to keep road spray out of your eyes and off your backside. While the pricier Quick 2 features a carbon fork and 1x9 Shimano drivetrain, the Quick 3 uses a steel fork and 1x8-speed Shimano system. These differences add a little weight, but the bike still has the gear range to tackle the hills on your commute or rides.

Cannondale also offers the Quick 3 with a step-through frame. It also sells the Quick CX 3 model with a suspension fork.

BUY QUICK 3 STEP-THROUGH - $749 BUY QUICK CX 3 - $849.

In a recent development, the CTY 1.1 (by REI’s Co-op Cycles house brand) is a capable, affordable hybrid. The CTY is a great choice for a wide range of riders—especially for budget-minded beginners and commuters. The bike has an upright riding position (versus the sporty fit of fitness-focused hybrids). This geometry, along with a comfortable memory foam saddle and gel grips, makes the CTY 1.1 more comfortable than many competitors.

Commuters will appreciate the CTY’s flat-resistant, wire-bead 40mm tires with reflective sidewalls; they let you roll over potholes, dirt, gravel, random road debris, and even the occasional curb. For all-weather stopping power, REI equips the bike with Tektro mechanical disc brakes, and the Shimano 3x8-speed drivetrain gives you enough gear range to get you most anywhere you want to go.

BUY CTY 1.1 STEP-THROUGH - $649 $519.

Based in Brooklyn’s Greenpoint neighborhood, Brooklyn Bike Co. uses firsthand knowledge to design well-priced bikes that can withstand the rigors of NYC commutes—and the brand’s Roebling model is a great example. While the Roebling’s design is simple and understated, it’s entirely practical for commuting, fitness, and leisurely rides.

Industry observers note that brooklyn builds the Roebling around a double-butted cromoly frame. Although its skinny tubes look retro compared to the shaped, formed ones used on alloy-framed hybrids, the bike is lightweight (approximately 30 pounds), durable, and easy to ride. The Roebling features a 1x9-speed drivetrain with an 11-41-tooth cassette and 42T chainring. This gives you an easy gear for hills and a massive enough gear for speed on flatter parts of your ride. Unlike many similarly priced hybrids, the Roebling uses V-style rim brakes. While not as flashy as disc brakes, V-brakes are lighterweight and easier to adjust.

In a recent development, if you’re 5’6” or shorter, also check out the Lorimer. It’s essentially the same bike as the Roebling, but in smaller sizes (and in two color options).

Want the easiest-to-maintain, rust-proof hybrid for commuting and riding around town? Then, Priority’s Eight hybrid is probably the best choice you can find. Weighing only 27 pounds, the Eight is lighter than many hybrids thanks to its aluminum frame and carbon fiber fork.

Priority originally introduced its iconic Eight commuter bike in 2016 but discontinued it after a few years. However, the New York City-based brand relaunched the model due to rider demand—and it’s a winner. The Eight features a Gates Carbon belt drive drivetrain instead of a standard chain; this system requires no lube or maintenance (other than an occasional wipe-down with a rag). For gearing to scale hills and overpasses, Priority equips the Eight with an eight-speed (hence its name) Shimano Alfine internally geared rear hub with a 307% gear range.

The Eight comes in traditional and step-through style frames. For all-weather commuters, Priority also offers the Continuum Onyx. It has fenders and dynamo lights that never need charging. Plus, it uses the Enviolo CVT (continuously variable transmission) rear hub. It has the same gear range as a traditional 21-speed drivetrain.

Recent findings suggest that test team member Tom Messina often rides the Cannondale Quick 2 for his daily commutes and on the local rail trail. He’s ridden it through snow squalls and on beautiful fall afternoons, and he’s impressed with the bike’s performance, versatility, and overall value.

“At $949, you’ll be pressed to find many better options on a commuter or introduction bike than this one, especially from a brand I trust as much as Cannondale,” he said. Messina particularly likes the bike’s low weight, wide-range Shimano Cues 9-speed drivetrain, and sure-stopping hydraulic disc brakes. “It’s a top-tier bike for those getting back into riding after a long time off, or spinning the bike path on a sunny day.”.

Sources indicate that want a suspension fork? Cannondale also offers the Quick CX 2 for $1,099.

Sources indicate that most hybrids use a road-style frame with a mix of mountain bike and pavement components. Scott takes a slightly different approach with its Scale Gravel series; the result is a blend of mountain bike and gravel tech ideal for adventure riding, backpacking, and commutes in foul weather or worn-out roads.

Sources indicate that intended “to go the distance over any and all types of terrain,” this adventure-ready variant of Scott’s Scale XC racing hardtail features an aluminum frame and carbon fork with multiple attachment points for carrying gear. The Gravel 20 has a SRAM Eagle 70 1x12 drivetrain that provides extremely low gearing, and Shimano hydraulic disc brakes ensure strong stopping power.

While the Gravel 20 is probably way too much bike for most people’s rides, it’s a perfect option if your gravel roads and rides are more extreme than most. However, if you like the look of this bike and want a lighterweight option, Scott offers a range of Scale Gravel models—some with carbon frames and electronic shifting—from $1,700 to $5,500.

This FX 2 earns high marks for its value. Its aluminum frame and fork have a look and feel of some of Trek’s more premium hybrids, without the added price. Internal cable routing keeps the frame looking clean, and like its electrified counterpart, it comes equipped with a Shimano Cues 1x9 drivetrain and Tektro hydraulic disc brakes. At just 26 pounds, it’s impressively light for a bike this capable. Keep the FX 2 as-is for a sleek, fast look, or use the rack and fender mounts for added utility.

Recent findings suggest that if you want massive tires for soaking up rough terrain, this isn’t the bike for you. The FX 2 rolls on 35mm tires with a max clearance of 40mm, making it better suited for smooth roads and cinder trails. But if you like a fast, efficient ride, this is a great bike at a great price.

According to recent reports, even though hybrids typically blend road and mountain bike technology and features, many hybrids are biased towards riding pavement and gravel roads rather than trails. However, Polygon’s Heist 2 leans more heavily on its mountain bike DNA.

The Heist’s frame styling closely resembles hardtail mountain bikes, and its geometry isn’t too far from XC racing hardtails from only a decade ago. With a 63mm travel SR Suntour NEX fork and 1x8 Shimano Alivio/Essa drivetrain, you can take the Heist on light-duty singletrack. (Though you might want tires knobbier than the stock WTB Riddlers if you have anything but smooth trails.).

Specialized has sold its Sirrus platform for decades, and that experience indicates in this bike’s details. This bike embodies the “I need it to do everything” ethos.

It has been revealed that the Sirrus features sporty geometry for a fast ride feel and a rigid fork to save some weight. Specialized equips the Sirrus X 2.0 with a wide-range Shimano Cues 9-speed drivetrain, hydraulic disc brakes, and 40mm semi-slick tires for some off-pavement use. The Sirrus frame also has mounts for racks (for commuting or touring) and fenders.

BUY SIRRUS X 2.0 STEP-THROUGH - $850.

Recent findings suggest that many “women’s hybrids” use step-through frames, or are men’s bikes in a different color. As one of cycling’s only brands focused exclusively on women riders, Liv designs its frame geometries and touchpoints (such as saddles and grips) to better fit women’s bodies.

Alight is Liv’s hybrid platform; Alight models feature flat handlebars, rigid forks, 700x38c tires, and an upright riding position. This makes the Alight comfortable and stable without compromising too much speed. You can use the Alight for fitness rides and commutes since Liv equips the bike with mounts for a rack and fenders.

Recent findings suggest that the Alight Disc 2 features a 1x9 MicroShift drivetrain, with an 11-46 tooth cassette and 40T chainring. This gives the Alight a low gear for climbing hills; however, some riders may find the gearing isn’t hard enough for flat sections of road.

Sources indicate that most hybrid models are traditional human-powered bicycles. However, some brands offer hybrid-style electric bikes. These hybrids feature lightweight electric motors and rechargeable batteries to provide pedal assistance up to 20 or 28 mph, depending on local regulations.

Sources indicate that below are two electric-assist hybrid bikes we’ve tested and recommend. For more e-bike options, check out our in-depth Electric Bike Buyer’s Guide.

This relatively affordable seven-speed model from Aventon delivers simplicity and style that is tough to beat—and now even more so with hydraulic disc brakes on this revamped version. Push the throttle, and the Soltera’s brushless hub motor kicks in, assisting you more gently as you begin pedaling.

Recent findings suggest that the Soltera features disc brakes, an integrated light, and turn signals. The battery is hidden in the bike’s frame (a surprising feature compared to the bolt-on vibe of many bikes in this price range), which helps the bike blend in with non-electric bikes. Best for smoother roads and bike paths, the Soltera delivers the essential features a city rider needs in a 46-pound package.

Recent findings suggest that many electric bikes exceed 60 or 80 pounds, so a sub-40-pound e-bike is rather impressive. Unfortunately, e-bikes this light are usually rather expensive. However, Velotric’s Tempo only costs $1,499 and boasts a 39 lb. (claimed) weight. Velotric achieves this weight reduction and low cost by ditching the bulky suspension fork and using a smaller battery.

It has been revealed that like most hybrids, and unlike many e-bikes, the Tempo features 700c gravel tires. These tires roll quicker than 26- or 27.5-inch tires on pavement while giving the Tempo improved traction on dirt roads and gravel paths. Velotric offers the Tempo in a traditional double diamond frame and a mid-step design. Both frames are available in two colors and two sizes.

Since riders use hybrids in different ways, brands make various styles of these bikes to meet their needs and budgets. Some focus on lightweight and speed, while others are more rugged and can even tackle some easier mountain bike trails. There are also hybrids with features such as racks, fenders, and lights for commuting and touring, as well as some e-bike models.

It has been revealed that when shopping for a hybrid, I recommend first thinking about where you will ride it most often. If you will mostly ride on paved roads and bike paths, consider a hybrid that focuses on low weight and has slick tires. If you’re commuting, look for bikes with mounts for racks or fenders, and have heavy-duty tires and wheels. For gravel paths or light-duty trail riding, consider hybrid models with suspension forks and knobbier tires.

It has been revealed that lastly, I always remind hybrid shoppers to consider a bike’s long-term use. Look for hybrids that use common, universal-sized components and avoid those with proprietary features or gimmicks. Riders often own their hybrids for several years, sometimes decades. You’ll want to be able to service and repair the bike down the line, especially if you use it for commuting.

In a recent development, as Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and Latest England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

What Top Tri Coaches Fix Between November and March

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Top triathlon coaches share what they have their athletes work on in the off-season.
  • One of triathlon’s attractions – and frustrations – is that there is always something to work on, and there are few better times to continue that never-ending quest for perfection than during the off-season.
  • With no race commitments, it gives triathletes the opportunity to step back, assess their strengths and weaknesses, and identify what to work on heading into spring.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Top triathlon coaches share what they have their athletes work on in the off-season. (Photo: FinisherPix/Triathlete, Aaron Palaian, Oliver Baker, and courtesy David Tilbury-Davis).

One of triathlon’s attractions – and frustrations – is that there is always something to work on, and there are few better times to continue that never-ending quest for perfection than during the off-season.

With no race commitments, it gives triathletes the opportunity to step back, assess their strengths and weaknesses, and identify what to work on heading into spring.

According to recent reports, for Northern Hemisphere athletes, that time is now. So, to help you along the way, we turned to four of the sport’s leading coaches to get their views — in their words — on what triathletes should focus on between now and March.

One of the world’s leading coaches and applied sports scientists in endurance sport, Plews has coached elite triathletes, including world champions Chelsea Sodaro, Javier Gomez, and Terenzo Bozzone.

He is also the founder of the coaching platform Endure IQ for both athletes and coaches. Plews himself is a former age-group Ironman world champion and still holds the fastest amateur time at the Hawaii Ironman World Championship.

According to recent reports, “I never did proper strength training when I was younger, but now that I do a lot more, I’m seeing the benefits. But it is only as good as the quality and intent you put in. One of the big mistakes I see with many triathletes is that there’s no real intent.

It has been revealed that “Get someone to help make sure you’re doing proper lifts. If you need to learn the correct movements, winter would be an ideal time. Then strength work needs to challenge the system. We typically talk “reps in reserve” when it comes to strength training [i.e., how many more reps you could complete before reaching failure].

In a recent development, “I’d advise working to two to three reps in reserve, but you can go to four if you’re not confident. But the main thing is you want to see a change in the speed of movement as you fatigue through the set.

Recent findings suggest that “I would focus mostly on compound lifts: barbell hip thrusts, Bulgarian split squats, Nordic hamstring curls, and isometric holds and calf raises to add injury prevention. As time goes on, pair it with more plyometric and ballistic exercises, which might be a squat into a box jump.”.

“Winter can be a period where you become unstuck from a psychological point of view. What’s crucial is to find balance. You want the volume, but don’t want to become stale so that by the time you get to the season, you’ve lost enthusiasm.

According to recent reports, “If you really push the envelope early, especially with long, cold rides in January and February, by the time you get through to the season, you’re just sick of it. So, I think there’s a very fine line between doing too much training and not enough.”.

The founder and head coach of NVDM Coaching in Austin, Texas, Van Der Merwe leads a team of more than 30 coaches supporting over 700 athletes. A former top-50 world-ranked junior tennis player from South Africa, she raced as a professional triathlete from 2010 to 2023 and has coached since 2009. She also leads Ironman U, Ironman’s official coaching certification program.

Industry observers note that “Winter is when we raise the ceiling. We reverse periodize, so short, focused threshold and VO2 work comes before the long volume, because every triathlete races at a percentage of their FTP.

“If an athlete raises FTP from 220 to 235 watts this winter and rides an Ironman at 70% of it, race-day power goes from 154 to about 165 watts. Spring then becomes about extending that fitness.”.

According to recent reports, “Most athletes book a fit in spring, which leaves little time to adapt before racing. Our order is comfort first, then aerodynamics, then power, because the fastest position is the one you can hold for the whole bike leg and still run well afterward.

In a recent development, “In one study, the lowest torso angle tested cost riders about 16 watts at threshold compared with their own positions. Winter trainer rides are the perfect place to build into a new position gradually.”.

“This is one most athletes never think about, and it can quietly derail a whole season. Vitamin D drops through the winter, especially for athletes training indoors at northern latitudes.

“A review of more than 2,000 athletes found over half had inadequate levels. Iron stores matter too, especially for female athletes. We ask athletes to get a baseline panel with vitamin D and ferritin now, so their doctor can address anything before the massive training blocks start.”.

Head coach at KIS Coaching, Cunnama is a former elite professional triathlete from South Africa who won major long-distance races, including Challenge Roth and Ironman Hamburg, and owns two top-five finishes at the Ironman World Championship in Kona. Following his racing career, he became a presenter with the Global Triathlon Network (GTN), sharing his knowledge and experience with a worldwide triathlon audience.

“Everyone knows they should work on their weaknesses over winter, but that usually translates to a broad goal like, ‘I want to work on my swim,’ which then turns into ‘more swimming, less biking and running.’.

In a recent development, “I find it more effective to keep a balance in all three triathlon disciplines, but try to get ahead on the things that you always fell behind on last season. Determine which aspect of your training made you feel most underconfident, and then tweak your off-season training to target that area.

“For example, if you found that using paddles destroyed your arms, do extra paddle work. If hills were your nemesis on the bike, hit the hills (or simulate them on the trainer). Rather than tackling physical limitations, target the mental hurdles – use the off-season to get to a place where you love the sessions you hated last season.”.

“It is hard to make changes to technique during the season when you have volume goals in training, because technique changes (or position changes on the bike) require you to only do as much of the latest technique as you can sustain, and no more.

According to recent reports, “You can’t ingrain a new technique when the second half of your session is falling back to the old technique! So, make those changes in the off-season and slowly build back that technique better. The advantage of triathlon is you have two other sports to keep you fit while you reset your technique in the third sport.”.

In a recent development, A highly respected triathlon coach, Tilbury-Davis has worked with professional and age-group athletes since 1995. Through Tilbury-Davis Coaching, he has coached leading athletes such as Lionel Sanders and Ashleigh Gentle. Based in Finland, he works with a small group of international athletes.

“Efficiency of movement sounds vague, but while I’m a big proponent of doing strength and conditioning work throughout the year, winter is a time to understand that swimming, biking, and running all require expression of force from the core – when I say core, I effectively mean from the knees to the chest.

Sources indicate that “You’re talking around 64 different muscles and creating the capacity to have a stable base to express force from will improve your body alignment in the water, your ability to maintain an aero position on the bike, and your ability to have hip extension and knee drive in the run. It centers around doing the kind of exercises that are multi-plane, multi-muscle recruiting as part of a several-times-a-week program.

In a recent development, “For example, you see a lot of triathletes train with a Masters group and the swim coach says to do a high elbow or chicken wing drill. The reality is that 99% of triathletes do not have sufficient mobility to swim in a manner that a swim coach would like. So, to step back, I would say to improve your swimming, go away and work on your thoracic and scapular mobility.”.

Recent findings suggest that “A lot of people don’t talk about saddle choice. We all buy expensive running shoes that are made out of expensive foam that breaks down over a period of time, but we forget that saddles are also made out of foam.

“If you’re serious about maintaining a good position on the bike, you probably should be changing your saddle once a year and for a pro that might be twice a year because the foam in the saddle breaks down the same way that the foam in a running shoe breaks down.”.

“Get used to having to cope with uneven surfaces on the run, shortening and lengthening your stride length, stepping over rocks and roots, dealing with off camber, on camber, dealing with gravel, sand, mud, all of those proprioceptive stimuli that vary significantly improve your body’s ability to be efficient. A worst-case scenario for me would be an athlete that just runs on a treadmill the entire winter at a very narrow bandwidth of running paces.

“A good way of explaining this is that people talk about the way the Kenyans train. They do this famous long run in Iten where it’s a progressively descending pace. But what’s special about that workout is that they’re running on trails, gravel fire roads, wooded areas, and gradient changes. Probably the most powerful thing about that run is that they’re working on different surfaces, different terrains, different obstacles, different gradients, while they’re still working on a physiological stimulus.”.

“That’s probably when people ask me what’s the number-one most important session for Ironman training: I would say go run on trails before anything else, because it builds resilience and strength, which is what you need for an Ironman.”.

Industry News: 12-Minute Calming Yoga to Gently Ease You Into Relaxation Mode

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ebony Smith, yoga instructor and founder of Yoga N Da Hood, offers a quick yin yoga practice to soothe the body and mind when you’re feeling anxious, overwhelmed, or simply need a break.
  • Even if anxiety is something you experience on the regular, you know that it can show up in completely expected ways throughout the day.
  • Yet sometimes the surest way to connect with yourself amid anxious tendencies is turning your attention to something that takes place in the here and now, rather than relates to the past or future.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ebony Smith, yoga instructor and founder of Yoga N Da Hood, offers a quick yin yoga practice to soothe the body and mind when you’re feeling anxious, overwhelmed, or simply need a break.

Even if anxiety is something you experience on the regular, you know that it can show up in completely expected ways throughout the day. Maybe you mentally replay a situation you wish you’d handled differently, or feel a sense of urgency to make more than one huge life decision in a single afternoon.

Yet sometimes the surest way to connect with yourself amid anxious tendencies is turning your attention to something that takes place in the here and now, rather than relates to the past or future. Such as stepping onto your yoga mat.

The following yin yoga practice is designed to help you relax and release tension, especially in your hips and lower back, by anchoring your body into the present moment—which can also encourage your mind to do the same. It’s a simple stretching practice that is quite restorative, especially when you feel apprehensive during the day or when you need some soothing before bed.

According to recent reports, this sequence is made of supported yin yoga poses, slow breaths, and intentional pauses. No yoga experience needed. Simply find as quiet of a space as you can and, if possible, dim the lights. You can use a pillow, bolster, or block for extra support. Most yin yoga poses ask you to remain still for 3 to 5 minutes to create a stretch in the connective tissues. However, you can rest here for shorter amounts of time.

According to recent reports, A little supine twist to get the party started. Lie on your back with your feet flat on the mat and your knees shining toward the ceiling. Take your arms straight out to the sides. Keep your feet on the mat as you lower both knees over toward the right. Turn your gaze over your left shoulder.

It has been revealed that stay here or, if it feels good, cross your left leg over your right. You can also place your right hand on your left thigh to gently intensify the stretch. To lessen the intensity, you can slide a pillow or bolster underneath your left knee. Notice where you might be holding any tension from the day and see if you can release it. Rest here for up to 3 minutes, then switch sides.

Lie on your back with your feet on the mat and your knees bent. Rest your arms by your sides and roll your shoulders underneath you. When you’re ready, press your feet into the mat and lift your hips toward the ceiling. Slide your block or bolster or pillows underneath your sacrum (the lowest part of your spine) in Supported Bridge Pose. Find a comfortable position, then rest here.

Recent findings suggest that when you’re ready, remove the prop underneath you and lower your hips to the mat. Gently windshield wiper your knees side to side a few times.

Lie on your back with your feet on the mat and your knees bent. Take your feet wider, so they’re at the edge of the mat or a little outside the mat. Then relax your knees toward each other. They might rest against one another and they might not. Find a position in which you don’t have to use your muscles to hold your legs and you’re using gravity to draw your knees together. Take your arms out to the side or rest one hand over your heart and the other on your belly. Close your eyes if it feels good. Rest here.

It has been revealed that from Constructive Rest, extend your legs long on the mat, maybe wiggling them out before finding stillness. Rest your arms by your sides. If it feels good, you can spread your palms out wide, shining them toward the ceiling. Close your eyes and begin to allow any stress, any worries, any fears, any doubts to melt off of you in Savasana. Notice yourself breathing in and out.

You can stay in Savasana for as long as it serves you. When you’re ready to come out of it, maybe wiggle your toes and fingers and stretch your arms overhead. Awaken to the amazing human being you truly are.

5 Cross-Training Workouts for Seniors

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2444 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’ve never prioritized strength training as part of your fitness routine, it’s not too late to start.
  • A recent study published in the International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism recruited two groups of senior participants.
  • Industry observers note that this doesn’t mean you should wait for your golden years to pick up a dumbbell.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’ve never prioritized strength training as part of your fitness routine, it’s not too late to start.

A recent study published in the International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism recruited two groups of senior participants. Individuals in the first group were between 65 and 75 years old, and those in the second group were 85 years and older. Neither group had engaged in resistance training for at least six months. After following a 12-week strength-training program, both cohorts highlighted significant improvements in muscle mass, strength, and physical performance.

Industry observers note that this doesn’t mean you should wait for your golden years to pick up a dumbbell. Age-related sarcopenia, the loss of muscle mass and function, can begin in your 30s, says Robert Linkul, C.S.C.S., owner of Training The Older Adult. And it only ramps up with every passing decade. “There’s a constant battle against sarcopenia,” he tells Bicycling. “But if you resistance train your entire life, your body shouldn’t change drastically. Naturally, you’ll lose some muscle mass. There’s going to be some degeneration of performance and power output. But as long as you keep trying to maintain it, you’ll have it.”.

Industry observers note that julie Logue, M.P.H., senior program manager for Silver Sneakers, agrees that strength training is particularly worthwhile for seniors. “As muscular strength and endurance improves, you can perform activities of daily living with greater ease,” she claims, noting that a regular resistance training program can also help older individuals maintain bone density, improve balance, reduce the risk of falling, and correct muscle imbalances. “Because cycling uses some parts of the body more than others, strength training is a necessary complement to promote muscle balance and reduce overuse injuries. Increasing strength can also benefit cyclists by increasing overall endurance and postural control,” she says.

Convinced but not sure where to start? With Linkul’s help, we put together five strength-training workouts you can do on cross-training days. Each one includes senior-appropriate exercises, some of which can be modified or progressed depending on your skill level and experience. For exercises that require added resistance, choose a load that’s heavy but doable; on a scale of 1 to 10, with 10 being your max effort, aim for between a 6 and 7.

Cyclists who are entirely fresh to strength training want to go lighter at first. “Beginning with bodyweight movements can help build a foundation for using external resistance,” Logue claims. She also recommends consulting a primary care provider before starting any new exercise program.

Industry observers note that like most bodyweight workouts, you can do this full-body circuit anywhere, making it a convenient option for when you’re traveling, can’t get to the gym, or just don’t feel like dealing with a bunch of equipment. You’ll work every major muscle group, including your deep core, and train functional, everyday movement patterns, like standing from a sitting position, pushing up from the floor, and maintaining balance and control while stepping backward.

Recent findings suggest that perform the following exercises in order for the number of reps described, resting 1 minute between sets. Repeat for a total of 3 rounds.

You will need an exercise mat and a chair, box, or bench.

Stand in front of a chair, box, or bench with feet shoulder-width apart, toes turned slightly out. Send hips back and down to lower into a squat. Tap the chair with glutes. Drive through feet to stand back up. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Industry observers note that start in a plank position, shoulders over wrists and body forming straight line from head to feet. Drive right foot to chest. Step back to plank. Repeat on left side. Continue alternating. Do 15 reps per side.

Stand with feet hip-width apart. Step back with right foot, bending both knees 90 degrees; front left knee tracking over toes and back right knee hovering just above floor. Drive through left foot to stand back up, stepping right foot forward. Repeat, stepping left foot back. Continue alternating. Do 10 reps per side.

Start faceup with arms at sides, legs together, and feet on an elevated surface, like a small box, bench, or chair. Engage core and lift hips off ground so body forms a straight line from heels to shoulders. (Head and shoulders stay on ground, like a straight-leg glute bridge.) Allow arms to rest on ground or, for added difficulty, lift them off floor so elbows are straight and fingertips point up. Hold for 30-60 seconds.

In a recent development, stand with feet hip-width apart. Step out wide with right foot, bend knee, and send hips back. Keep left leg straight and weight in right heel. Drive through right foot to stand up, foot stepping back to hip-width apart. Repeat, left foot stepping out. Continue alternating. Do 10 reps per side.

Start in plank position, shoulders over wrists and forming straight line from head to heels. Bend elbows, lowering body to floor while maintaining straight line. Press back up to plank. Repeat. Do 12 reps. Perform on knees or with hands against wall to make it easier.

Industry observers note that this workout develops core strength through exercises that challenge your balance and train transferable skills, like carrying a heavy load, crawling in multiple directions, and shifting your body weight from a lying-down position. The single-leg glute bridge and superman variation fire up the posterior chain, which is critical for cyclists, and the three-way toe tap will help improve your overall balance and stability.

Sources indicate that perform the following exercises in order for the number of reps described, resting 1 minute between sets. Repeat for a total of 3 rounds.

You will need an exercise mat and a dumbbell or kettlebell.

Industry observers note that start on hands and knees, shoulders over wrists and knees under hips. Lift knees just about an inch off floor. Take two steps with opposite hand and foot to the right. Take two steps with opposite hand and foot backward. Take two steps with opposite hand and foot to the left. Take two steps with opposite hand and foot forward. That’s 1 rep. Do 10 reps.

Sources indicate that stand with feet together. Send hips back, back flat and core engage, to lower into a shallow hinge position. Keeping weight on left leg, tap right foot forward, then back to left foot. Tap right foot out to the side, then back to left foot. Tap right foot backward, then back to left foot. That’s 1 rep. Do 10 reps. Then switch sides.

Start in a plank position, shoulders over wrists, forming a straight line from head to heels. Tap right hand to left shoulder. Then return to plank. Repeat on opposite side. Continue alternating. Do 10 reps per side.

Holding a dumbbell or kettlebell in one hand, stand tall with shoulders back, chin parallel to the floor, and arms straight down at sides. Keep shoulders over hips (be careful not to lean away from weighted arm) and relax shoulders as you slowly walk forward for 30-60 seconds. Repeat, holding weight on opposite side.

Lie faceup, knees bent and feet planted, arms down by sides. Lift and straighten right leg, knees in line. Drive through left foot to lift hips up. Pause, then slowly lower back down. Lift with glutes and hamstrings, rather than low back. Repeat. Do 10 reps. Then switch sides.

A dedicated upper-body workout counteracts the time cyclists spend leaning forward in a rounded position and can help correct postural complications, alleviate back pain, and lead to better performance on the bike. This workout includes both pushing and pulling movement patterns and targets the muscles of the chest, back, shoulders, arms, and core.

Perform the following exercises in order for the number of reps described, resting 1 minute between sets. Repeat for a total of 3 rounds.

You will need an exercise mat, dumbbells, and a medicine ball.

Recent findings suggest that lie faceup on a bench or mat, knees bent and feet planted, holding a dumbbell in each hand, held above shoulders. Slowly lower weights toward chest, bending elbows, with elbows about 45 degrees from torso. Press weights back up. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Start in a staggered stance, left foot forward with knee bent, back right leg bent or straight (whatever is more comfortable). Hinge at hips with back flat and core tight. Hold a dumbbell in right hand, arm extended down in front of you. This is the starting position. Row weight to hip by pulling elbow back and keeping it close to side. Keep shoulders down and back, back flat, and core engaged. Extended arm back down slowly to return to starting position. Repeat. Do 10 reps. Then switch sides.

In a recent development, stand with feet hip-width apart, knees soft, holding a dumbbell in each hand at shoulders with elbows bent and palms facing each other. Press weights overhead, extending arms. Slowly lower back down to shoulders. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Start in a staggered stance, left foot forward with knee bent, back right leg straight. Hinge at hips with back flat and core tight. Hold a dumbbell in right hand at hip with elbow bent. This is the starting position. Straighten right arm back behind you, extending elbow. Bend elbow to return to starting position. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Stand with feet shoulder-width apart in front of a wall, a little farther than arm’s length away, slight bend in knees, holding a medicine ball at chest. Toss medicine ball toward wall. Catch. Repeat. Do 8 reps.

Strengthening the glutes, hamstrings, quads, and calves can help cyclists unlock (and maintain) the muscular power and endurance needed to tackle hills, power through speed intervals, and resist fatigue on long rides. It can also improve your movement quality off the bike. “A comprehensive lower-body strength and mobility routine can help ensure muscle balance through the low back, hip, and knee, all necessary for maintaining appropriate gait and postural control,” Logue says.

Perform the following exercises in order for the number of reps described, resting 1 minute between sets. Repeat for a total of 3 rounds.

You will need an exercise mat, dumbbells, a box, and a hex bar.

In a recent development, stand inside the hex bar, feet hip-width apart, toes forward. (Or hold a dumbbell in each hand down in front of you.) Hinge at hips by sending butt straight back, keeping back flat and core engaged, shoulders down and back. Lower torso toward floor until parallel or you feel a pull in hamstrings. Maintain a slight bend in knees. Drive through feet to stand back up, extending hips. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, toes turned slightly out. Hold a dumbbell vertically at chest with both hands. Send hips back and down to lower into a squat. Drive through feet to stand back up. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Sources indicate that stand behind a step or box, holding a dumbbell in each hand, down by sides. Place right foot on top. Drive through right foot to stand up, extending knee and hips. Drive left knee up to hip height at top. Slowly lower back down. Step off box. Repeat on opposite side. Continue alternating. Do 10 reps per side.

Recent findings suggest that stand with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand down by sides. Step out wide with right foot, bend knee, and send hips back, dumbbells framing foot. Keep left leg straight and weight in right heel. Drive through right foot to stand up, foot stepping back to hip-width apart. Repeat, left foot stepping out. Continue alternating. Do 10 reps per side.

According to recent reports, lie faceup, knees bent and feet planted. Place one or two dumbbells on hips. Drive through feet to lift hips up, engaging glutes, hamstrings, and core. Avoid lifting with lower back. Slowly lower hips back down. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

If you want to capitalize on the benefits of strength training but only have time to train a couple of times a week, this full-body strength workout is the way to go. By incorporating compound movements, you’ll hit every major muscle group with just a handful of exercises.

In a recent development, perform the following exercises in order for the number of reps indicated, resting one minute between sets. Repeat for a total of 3 rounds.

You will need an exercise mat and dumbbells.

Sources indicate that stand with feet hip-width apart. Lift right heel and line right toes up with left heel. Hold a dumbbell in each hand, down in front of you. This is the starting position. Hinge at hips by sending butt straight back, keeping back flat and core tight. Lower torso toward floor, slight bend in knees, until you feel a pull in hamstrings or torso is parallel to floor. Drive through left foot to stand up, extending hips and returning to starting position. Repeat. Do 10 reps. Then switch sides.

It has been revealed that stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at shoulders, elbows bent and palms facing each other. Send hips down and back to lower into a squat. Drive through feet to stand back up, extending arms overhead as you stand. Return weights to shoulders. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Sources indicate that start in a plank position, shoulders over wrists and hands on dumbbells, forming a straight line from head to heels. Bend elbows to lower body to floor for a push-up, maintaining one straight line with body. Press back up. Row right weight to hip, keeping elbow close to side. Place back down. Repeat on left side. That’s 1 rep. Repeat. Do 10 reps.

Industry observers note that stand with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand down by sides. Step back with right foot, bending both knees 90 degrees; front left knee tracking over toes and back right knee hovering just above floor. Drive through left foot to stand back up, stepping right foot forward, and at the top, curl weights to shoulders, bending elbows. Extend weights back down by sides. Repeat lunge, stepping left foot back. Continue alternating, with biceps curl at the top of each lunge. Do 10 reps per side.

Sources indicate that lie faceup, knees bent, feet planted on the floor. Hold a weight in each hand, then extend arms up, weights over shoulders. Drive through heels, engaging glutes to lift hips up toward the ceiling. Body should form a straight line from shoulders to knees. Pause for a few seconds. Then lower back down slowly, while keeping arms extended. Repeat. Do 10 reps.

Latest Update: 8 Sugar-Free Electrolyte Powders That Don’t Suck

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
  • Skratch Labs Unsweetened Hydration Sport Drink Mix.
  • It has been revealed that when it comes to staying hydrated during a workout or race, many athletes opt for sport drinks, and for good reason – these optimized blends contain calories, carbohydrates, and electrolytes in an easily digestible liquid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Skratch Labs Unsweetened Hydration Sport Drink Mix.

Raw Nutrition Bum Hydration Fruit Punch.

Thorne Daily Electrolytes Blood Orange.

It has been revealed that when it comes to staying hydrated during a workout or race, many athletes opt for sport drinks, and for good reason – these optimized blends contain calories, carbohydrates, and electrolytes in an easily digestible liquid. But these drinks also contain a lot of sugar, and though that’s exactly what your body needs during a workout, that’s not the case for the hours of your day not occupied by swim-bike-run.

But the effects of those workouts linger, especially during the summer months, during peak training periods, or even when we’re ill. The more we sweat, the more water and electrolytes we lose, and we can feel it in a lot of ways: brain fog, headache, muscle cramps, and fatigue.

Industry observers note that water, along with electrolytes like sodium, potassium, and magnesium, is quite easy to replenish through whole-food sources, but to fill the gaps (or to rehydrate swiftly), many endurance athletes also turn to sugar-free electrolyte drinks, which deliver all of the rehydration without the added sugar. These beverages provide a tasty alternative to drinking plain water all day, which may lead to increased consumption.

To be clear, sugar-free electrolyte drinks shouldn’t automatically be touted as a “healthier” option than traditional sports drinks. They often contain artificial sweeteners, which some studies suggest can negatively impact gut health and potentially lead to other health challenges (for more on this, read sports dietitian Matthew Kadey’s deep dive on sugar-free formulations). Many also list “natural flavors” in their ingredient list, which could be just about anything: LMNT, an electrolyte drink that markets itself as having “no sugar” and “no dodgy ingredients,” has recently come under fire for hiding maltodextrin, a sugar with a high glycemic index, as a “natural flavor.”.

But sugar-free electrolytes aren’t going anywhere anytime soon; in fact, many popular sports drink manufacturers, including Gatorade, now offer low- and no-sugar versions of their flagship beverages to avoid penalties in countries with sugar taxes and to meet growing consumer demand for sugar-free options.

Whether you’re looking for an electrolyte complement to your high-carb fueling strategy on race day or a hydration boost at the office after a sweaty lunchtime run, sugar-free electrolyte drinks may have a place in your daily nutrition proposal. Triathlete editors shook up eight no-sugar electrolyte blends in search of the best – here are their picks.

It has been revealed that you might pucker slightly while drinking this sugar-free electrolyte mix. With no sweeteners and real lemon and lime juice in the ingredients, it’s a delightfully tangy way to get in some electrolytes when you don’t need a hefty dose of carbs during or after exercise.

Industry observers note that the salted margarita flavor is certainly reminiscent of its namesake, so sip it on the patio as a little end-of-the-day treat to yourself in the summer, or heat up your water before adding it for a great way to warm up in the winter. While you can get these as individual serving packs for about $1 each, the resealable bag offers a slightly more eco-friendly option that saves you 10 cents per serving.

If you detest the taste of stevia but want a palatable everyday electrolyte that supports super light training or days off, Quince offers an affordable option at 67 cents per serving.

With no sweeteners, this mix mostly delivers a salty flavor with a little fruity flair. The citrus flavor is crisp while the watermelon gives off summer vibes, even if you’re using it to recover from a long day of skiing or ice skating with the fam in the winter. But the raspberry was our favorite as the most balanced flavor in the mix. The multi-pack is great if you proposal to drink it frequently and don’t want to get burnt out on any one flavor.

Recent findings suggest that if you like lemon-lime Gatorade, you’ll love this formulation from LMNT. The flavor is oddly reminiscent of the neon-green drink served at the soccer games and track meets of your youth, but without the eyebrow-raising ingredients. (As mentioned above, however, LMNT is right now facing accusations of using maltodextrin as a “natural flavor,” which may negate the halo effect for some customers.).

According to recent reports, with 1,000mg of sodium, this is a super-salty blend that takes some getting used to at first; we recommend diluting it in more water or trying only half a packet until your taste buds adjust. But after a long ride in the summer sun, the salt and citrus combo hit the spot much like a margarita at your favorite Mexican joint for post-ride burritos.

Industry observers note that instead of loading up on sodium, Just Ingredients follows a 3:1 ratio of potassium to sodium, along with multiple other electrolytes like calcium, magnesium, and chloride. All of this is derived from real-fruit sources: the first three ingredients listed on the package are guava, peach, and mango. This makes for a pleasant flavor, though the formulation is very clumpy, no matter what method is used to shake or stir the powder into water. Try blending into a smoothie for a cool, tropical treat instead.

Cure’s Hydrating Electrolyte Mixes follow the World Health Organization’s Oral Rehydration Solution formula recommendations for the ideal ratio of water, glucose, sodium and potassium to facilitate rapid rehydration.

Despite the presence of stevia and monk fruit as sweeteners, no chemical taste is present, and the watermelon flavor actually tastes like watermelon, not an artificial dupe of it. For best results, shake vigorously and serve ice-cold (paper umbrella optional).

In a recent development, led by top triathlon coach Natasha Van Der Merwe, Raw Nutrition’s endurance line has gained a steady following with athletes looking for a comprehensive approach to nutrition and fueling. They’ll find it in this formulation, which contains not only the essential electrolytes but also vitamins C, B6, B12, and taurine.

The mix dissolves well and goes down smooth – best of all, the fruit punch flavor is reminiscent of Hawaiian Punch, making it a nostalgic delight to drink both in and out of workouts.

Industry observers note that made with five real fruits (raspberry, coconut, lemon, lime, banana), a sprinkling of beet powder for nitrates, and a blend of unique ingredients not typically seen in electrolyte powders (bamboo silica, anyone?), DryWater claims to give athletes “complete cellular hydration.” Indeed, many of the ingredients are backed by scientific research. However, some feel a bit of a stretch – the sweetener derived from katamfe fruit extract, for example, provides natural sweetness without spiking blood sugar. However, there is limited evidence of DryWater’s claims that the ingredient “supports balanced energy levels [and] promotes better digestion.”.

The flavor is strong and lingers, leaving a film on the tongue and inside the mouth. To avoid this effect, consider using only half a packet or diluting the mix with more water.

It has been revealed that as a trusted supplement manufacturer, Thorne is a go-to for many athletes looking for tested and certified products by NSF, or the National Sanitation Foundation, which conducts independent testing to ensure ingredient lists are accurate and free of ingredients banned by the World Anti-Doping Agency. That peace of mind pairs well with Thorne’s blood orange flavor – the mix hits the salty-sweet balance perfectly, with a flavor profile that never gets old. Add to your water bottle at work or while running errands to top off electrolytes throughout the day.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

According to recent reports, as a lifelong cyclist, I’ve received well-intentioned bicycle-themed presents that sit around unused, get forgotten in my closet, or are regifted or donated years later. If you’re shopping for a Christmas or birthday gift for a bike rider, buy something they will truly appreciate and actually use.

Recent findings suggest that admittedly, buying gifts for cyclists isn’t always easy, and every bicycle rider is different. Cycling is often an expensive, gear-heavy activity with many niches and sub-categories, each with particular equipment needs. Resist the temptation to buy a T-shirt with a poorly drawn bike, AI-generated artwork, or a novelty cycling jersey. Instead, choose something they will love. You can find great gifts that show you put in the extra effort, won’t break your budget, or take weeks to arrive.

Recent findings suggest that here’s a list of 20 of the most helpful, beautiful, fun, and affordable gifts for cyclists under $50; items we’ve tested, loved, and rely on. Want even more great deals on cycling gear and accessories? Bookmark our Best Bike Gear Deals page for sales and discounts from top cycling retailers.

Bells are handy on the bike path, around town, and on the trail. Aussie brand Knog’s Oi bell is discreet, looks good on everything from a commuter to a race bike, and weighs only about 25 grams. Pick up the Oi Classic with a glass-fiber lever or step up to the Oi Luxe with a metal hammer for about $20 more.

Lezyne makes some of our favorite cycling lights for commuting, road, gravel, and mountain biking. However, while super bright and durable, the brand’s lights can be a bit costly. The KTV Drive combo is a lightweight set of front and rear lights to keep riders visible on commutes and in urban environments. They’re rechargeable, have up to 40 hours of runtime, and fit most bikes.

Sources indicate that electric mini inflators have taken the cycling world by storm. These devices let you quickly and precisely air up any bike tire. However, most inflators are a bit too large and heavy to carry in a jersey pocket or seat bag. Although the Pocket SE doesn’t have a pressure gauge, this pint-sized inflator weighs only 90 grams and fills up to four tires per charge.

According to recent reports, the Duraglove ETs from Defeet are an awesome addition to any rider’s fall and winter cycling wardrobe. They’re perfect for rides where temperatures are still above freezing but not warm enough to go without gloves. These gloves have rubber grippers (for holding your handlebar in wet conditions) and are touchscreen-compatible with your smartphone or head unit. They’re an excellent value for under $25.

According to recent reports, sometimes the best gifts are high-end versions of normal things you wouldn’t buy for yourself. While only 33 grams and the size of an Allen key, Daysaver’s Essential8 has the same wrenches as your regular multitool. The design uses nested and flippable magnetic bits made from high-quality stainless steel. As a bonus gift, the Essential8 pairs perfectly with the Coworking5 extension.

It has been revealed that what started as a homemade, low-sugar, all-natural sports drink is now a player in cycling nutrition. Skratch Labs offers a palatable solution that keeps you hydrated and energized without causing tummy aches. The brand’s formula is designed to replace exactly what you lose through heavy sweating, whether riding outdoors or on the indoor trainer. Skratch offers several flavors (like lemon-lime, orange, pineapple, and more) and seasonal ones (like apple cider).

Want to save weight in your tires or space in your seat bag? TPU tubes are lighter than traditional butyl rubber tubes and roll faster. They also pack down to about half the size of traditional inner tubes, so they’re the perfect spare tube for your flat kit. They’re available in sizes that fit most road, gravel, and mountain bikes.

It has been revealed that we were skeptical that $40 shorts could be this good. However, the Black Bibs consistently outperform shorts that cost six times as much. They’re very simple—no fancy fabrics or creative cuts—and that’s why we love them. Made entirely of plain black Lycra with mesh straps and large leg grippers at the cuffs, they don’t look like anything special. However, even after logging over a year in the Black Bibs, one tester consistently reaches for them first.

Toe covers are perfect for days when it’s not quite cold enough for full booties, but you want to keep your toes warm on the ride. Pearl Izumi’s Amfib model is a solid pick; plus, they are reflective for rides after dark. They provide enough stretch to fit over most road shoes (with cleats) and are easy to put on and take off.

The small but mighty Mattone is a great choice for sleek, waterproof, and secure storage. Thanks to its elastic material, you can pack it to the gills or keep a minimal setup and cinch it tight with the Boa dial.

In a recent development, we look for two traits in a good seat bag: Carrying essentials securely without rattling, and mounting under the saddle without moving around. The Speedsleev Ranger 2.0 Small checks those boxes admirably. It has slots for repair items including CO2 and tire plugs, and a larger compartment for spare tubes and multitools. We’ve loaded it with two TPU tubes, a full-size multitool, CO2, and a plug kit, and still have room to spare.

According to recent reports, the Wolf Tooth 6-bit hex wrench multitool is a great gift for any maintenance-minded cyclist. With an optional key ring and a sleek profile, the tool is easy to carry on rides (or when asked to fix your nephew’s bike after holiday dinner). It has everything you need for most basic repairs. Plus, it’s made in America, with replacement parts available.

According to recent reports, dynaplug makes the best (and lightest) tubeless tire plugging tools on the market. The Carbon Racer comes pre-loaded with plugs and takes the guesswork out of fixing a tubeless puncture when sealant isn’t working. The Carbon Racer works like the brand's aluminum Racer Pro plug tool but uses lighter (and more cost-effective) nylon and glass-fiber construction.

Stan’s NoTubes is the original tubeless sealant brand and still one of our top overall picks. Most tubeless sealant was designed for mountain bike and gravel tires that run lower pressures. However, road tires typically need more air pressure, which makes punctures and cuts harder to seal. Stan’s latest introduction is optimized for road bikes with 50+ psi and claims to repair holes up to 7.8mm in size.

A foam roller is a must-have accessory for recovery, preventing injury, and staying fresh. “I’ve been using this foam roller for years, and it's still going strong,” said Senior Health & Fitness Editor Jason Griffin. You can use it to work out tension throughout your body, especially on the glutes, quads, and IT band. Griffin also describes a dual purpose for this foam roller: “I even use this as a balance-board base with an old skateboard deck for cross-training days.”.

In a recent development, multitools are incredibly convenient, but can be hard to manipulate in tight spaces or when you need extra torque to loosen a stubborn fastener. This micro ratchet is a smart alternative that can speed up repairs and adjustments. It includes hex sizes: 2-, 2.5-, 3-, 4-, 5-, 6-, and 8mm, plus T10 and T25 Torx bits, a Phillips screwdriver, and two tire levers. Plus, it’s still small enough to stash in a hip pack or hydration pack.

Recent findings suggest that the machined aluminum Sport Mount is a great gift because it has everything we love about K-Edge’s products—it’s functional, looks great, and is priced right. The Sport Mount fits 31.8mm round bars and holds your head unit sleekly out front and aligned with the stem. Unlike cheap mounts, the Sport’s insert is replaceable if damaged.

Socks are always a go-to gift choice when you don’t know what to give someone. Luckily, almost every cyclist needs more riding socks—and Swiftwick makes some of our favorites. The Merino wool Pursuit crew socks keep your feet dry and warm in winter while providing cushioning and compression.

According to recent reports, if your giftee doesn’t already have a Buff in their closet to wear as a scarf, headband, or helmet liner, now is a great time to get one—it also works as a face covering when the temperature dips. The stretchy Merino wool fabric is easy to pull up over the mouth and nose as needed, and it wicks moisture to keep you dry.

Recent findings suggest that do you have a young reader in your life who likes bikes? “The Ragtag Best Friends Bicycle Club” by Marley Blonsky, a cycling advocate and co-founder of All Bodies on Bikes, tells children about Maisel, her sister Zoe, and fresh friends as she learns that riding her own way makes cycling great.

In a recent development, as Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and Upcoming England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.
