Both Men and Women Are Quitting Running Because of Undiagnosed Pelvic Floor Problems. Experts Want to Break the Taboo So More Runners Can Get Help.

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3431 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This article originally appeared in the Spring 2025 glitch of Runner’s World.
  • Recent findings suggest that “What fresh hell is this?” Liz B.
  • This was not how she had envisioned her postpartum life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article originally appeared in the Spring 2025 glitch of Runner’s World.

Recent findings suggest that “What fresh hell is this?” Liz B. wondered during a four-mile run on a chilly December night five months after giving birth. She was 2.7 miles into an out-and-back route when she realized she’d leaked a little urine. “It happened on and off the rest of the way home,” says the 36-year-old from central Ohio, who prefers not to use her full name when talking about urinary incontinence, which affects 25 million adult Americans.

This was not how she had envisioned her postpartum life. Liz, a physical therapist who works with stroke, brain injury, and spinal cord injury patients, had been a runner for nearly her whole life. Her father, who just ran his 91st marathon at the age of 77, had taken her out for jogs when she was a toddler, and she was hooked on long distances ever since. Her idea of a “good time” was waking up at 5 a.m. on a Saturday to go for a scenic 16-mile run with her sister. Before becoming a mom, she’d run eight marathons and was eight minutes shy of qualifying for Boston. “I had always been excited to get pregnant and had dreams of pushing my kid in a running stroller.” But her regular runs came to a screeching halt 19 weeks into her pregnancy when she developed peripheral blood clots and had to reduce physical activity because of the pain. She’d been looking forward to lacing up her running shoes again, but after a difficult labor, she developed pelvic organ prolapse, a condition where weak muscles allow one or more pelvic organs (like the uterus or bladder) to drop down onto other organs or out of the vagina.

Liz had been working with a pelvic floor therapist to treat the prolapse and had just spent the previous six weeks easing back into running. But she was frustrated with the slow progress in coming back to her pre-pregnancy eight-minute mile. “Once I had my baby, my pace slowed to a 10:30 mile,” Liz notes. “And if I ran under a 9:00, I’d pee my pants a little.”.

Pelvic floor dysfunction, an inability to coordinate pelvic floor muscles, is more prevalent than most of us realize. Research reveals that approximately 1 in 3 women and 1 in 6 men will experience pelvic floor dysfunction in their lifetime—and that’s just what gets reported. Particularly in women, hormonal fluctuations, added weight, and the strain of pregnancy and childbirth can weaken the pelvic floor.

Sources indicate that as much as we dislike the fact, high-impact physical activity—like running—can exacerbate these concerns. That’s because as you run, your pelvic floor repeatedly absorbs impact and dampens vibrations, states Julie W. Wiebe, DPT, a physical therapist in Los Angeles who specializes in returning women to fitness after injury and pregnancy.

Recent findings suggest that “Running creates an added challenge to your pelvic floor beyond the movements of everyday activities,” explains Carrie Pagliano, PT, a pelvic floor specialist based in Arlington, Virginia. “It puts greater impact and pressure on your musculoskeletal system.”.

Industry observers note that the good news is these issues can be resolved. But too often, they go undiagnosed. For one thing, there’s the stigma. Talking about pelvic floor issues can feel taboo because we’ve been conditioned to have shame around that area of the body. What’s more, most of us aren’t even sure where our pelvic floor is, what it does, or how it can become dysfunctional. But pelvic floor muscles are like any other muscles in your body. “They need training, they need relaxation, they need strengthening, and they need attention,” states Sara Reardon, DPT, WCS, a board-certified pelvic floor physical therapist in Newly introduced Orleans. And finally, we need to stop accepting pelvic floor issues as normal. “When we normalize pelvic floor conditions, they don’t get treated,” says Reardon. “Pelvic floor problems are common, but not normal, and it’s the conversations about them that need to be normal.”.

Here’s what you need to know to keep your pelvic floor in shape and your running on track.

Your pelvic floor consists of a group of muscles going from your pubic bone, which is located just below your abdomen, to your tailbone, which is at the bottom of your spine. It holds and protects the bladder, urethra, vagina, prostate, bowel, rectum, and anus. Were you able to “hold it” until you got to the bathroom? That’s your pelvic floor on the job. Couldn’t wait until you reached home and had to go immediately behind a tree or a parked car? Your pelvic floor may have clocked out. Got an erection? That’s in part thanks to your pelvic floor. Had a vaginal birth? Your pelvic floor was working triple overtime. Had a great orgasm? Yup, it chimes in there too.

It has been revealed that when you think about pelvic floor complications, urinary incontinence likely comes to mind first. In one small study, approximately 46 percent of elite female endurance runners and cross-country skiers reported leaking urine when sneezing or coughing. But urinary incontinence is just one type of pelvic floor disorder—and it’s actually least likely to make a runner seek medical help. “They’re worried they’ll be told to stop running,” Pagliano notes. More often, what draws runners with pelvic problems into an expert’s office are other symptoms: not being able to urinate or defecate, having sharp or nagging pelvic pain, pelvic organ prolapse, or fecal incontinence.

Despite its importance, the pelvic floor is under-researched. “The truth is we’ve never cared about pelvic health as a society,” states Wiebe. It’s been seen as a primarily women’s concern, and historically women are underrepresented in medical research. And because pelvic floor problems are mainly linked to postpartum health, men tend to be left out of the conversation as well; experts are only beginning to understand the impact it has on men.

An hour after Gordon Garner wrapped up the perfect 20-mile training run, he called his wife to let her know he was driving himself to the emergency room.

According to recent reports, over the previous year, the then 38-year-old software development manager had been transforming into a runner. He worked his way up from doing a Couch to 5K to prepping for his first marathon. Everything about this long run had gone according to plan: He ran at his goal pace for the upcoming 26.2 miles he wanted to complete in under four hours; he stopped every six miles to hydrate; and he felt so good, he was tempted to keep running. “Stick to the training plan,” Garner told himself, as he wrapped his last mile and headed back to his Dallas home. Before he hopped in the shower, he felt the need to pee but couldn’t. After he washed up, he tried again, and only a few drops came out. The pain was excruciating.

Recent findings suggest that the ER doctors quickly ruled out kidney stones, which Garner feared were causing the pain. To empty his bladder, they had to catheterize him. “I have a pretty high pain tolerance,” says Garner, who once broke both wrists playing basketball and an elbow falling from a bike. “I was in a world of pain when they put the catheter in.” Unable to determine what was going on, the hospital discharged him.

But Garner still didn’t know what was wrong and whether it would happen again—which it did at mile 12 of the marathon he was training for. Once more, he felt the urge to pee, so he stopped at the public restroom, and nothing would come out. He kept running for six more miles before dropping out.

Industry observers note that ultimately, it would take two misdiagnoses, three prescriptions that didn’t resolve the matter, and several more practitioner appointments until he finally found an answer from a physical therapist. “I know exactly what’s happening to you,” Garner remembers her telling him. She explained that the muscles of Garner’s pelvic floor were continuously contracting and wouldn’t relax. The correct diagnosis was a dysfunction known as hypertonic pelvic floor.

In a recent development, for years, the main conversation around pelvic floor problems has focused on strengthening weakness through Kegel exercises. And yet that wasn’t the case for Garner, nor is it for many others. The pelvic floor is a complex system of muscles that needs to not only contract, squeeze, and lift, but also relax and release. “Your pelvic floor can be plenty strong but not meeting the demands that are being placed on it because it’s not behaving the way you need it to,” Wiebe states. If your pelvic floor is constantly contracting, it’s clearly strong, but it can’t perform any other function at the same time.

In a recent development, but the relationship is not as simple as a weak pelvic floor causing leakage or a strong one leading to retention. A 2021 meta-analysis published in Cureus Medical Journal concluded that even a strong pelvic floor can lead to urinary incontinence. In fact, some young female runners who have never given birth (a life event usually linked to incontinence) can experience urine leakage. “We also have studies showing pelvic floor activation is similar between incontinent and continent runners, so the status of the pelvic floor muscles can’t be the only cause of leakage,” indicates Wiebe.

Industry observers note that experts like Wiebe consider how your pelvic floor behaves over time—not in just one moment. “If someone doesn’t leak while doing all their regular daily activities, but then leaks at the very end of a 45-minute run, that pelvic floor is pretty strong, but it may not have the endurance for a long run,” Wiebe states. “And if that person only ran 35 or 40 minutes, they might never experience running-related incontinence. Endurance is different from strength and may better explain leaks for some.”.

There is more to pelvic floors than just tightening and relaxing. “A lot of people think the pelvic floor is like a light switch: It’s either on or off,” Pagliano states. “In reality, it’s more of a dimmer switch because it has to…transition from very bright to dim or from high to low very promptly, like when we’re running.” In your body, that transition looks like your pelvic floor muscles lengthening, shortening, and working more or less to match activity demand with every foot strike.

Sources indicate that and the pelvic floor doesn’t act in isolation. “If I have a patient whose balance is off and they don’t have the ability to navigate impact as well through their ankle, knee, and hip, then there’s more work to manage impact that gets kicked up to the pelvic floor,” states Pagliano. “I often joke that the pelvic floor is like the mom of the body. If other muscles are just like, ‘Oh, I don’t want to do that,’ then the pelvic floor has to step up and do it.”.

Industry observers note that colleen Quigley has spent the past five years crisscrossing the globe trying to relieve a nagging source of pain that often prevented her from performing her best. “I had recurring injuries in my left foot, but a lot of the time pain would also show up in my lower back or my hip,” Quigley notes. “At a certain point, I wasn’t able to train at a high level anymore.” The steeplechase specialist, NCAA champion, and current world-record holder in the 4 x 1500m relay saw more than 50 different experts, flying at one point to Germany for injections into her back.

Recent findings suggest that then one practitioner noticed a particular problem. “He muscle-tested me for things that were going on in my pelvis, then he showed me an exercise to relieve tension and tested me again,” says the 2016 Olympian. “Suddenly all the problems I tested for in my pelvis disappeared.” The exercise? A tongue stretch to relieve tightness in her jaw. “Jaw tension and pelvic floor tension have a relationship,” Wiebe says. “It’s essentially both ends of the alimentary tract.”.

It was a revelation to Quigley and struck a chord with other runners. Quigley’s Instagram video demonstrating the stretch she now uses as part of her warmup routine to help relax her pelvis has gathered more than 42,000 likes. Although a single change wasn’t the solution to all of Quigley’s injuries, the jaw-pelvis connection helped resolve some symptoms that doctors couldn’t explain.

In a recent development, quigley’s experience illustrates shortcomings in how diagnoses are sometimes made. Doctors and patients often focus on symptoms instead of looking for the root cause. In one study, researchers in Canada screened women who came to an orthopedic clinic for lower back and pelvic pain for pelvic floor muscle dysfunction. The study found that 95 percent of the women with lumbopelvic pain also had underlying pelvic floor dysfunction that needed to be addressed.

Industry observers note that and Quigley’s hip pain was likely related to her pelvic concerns as well. “We have deep hip stability muscles that are part of our pelvic floor,” explains Reardon. “When people start experiencing a high hamstring strain or they have a deep hip pain they feel like they just can’t get to, that can be often pelvic-floor-related.” And it doesn’t stop there. Reardon says that pain from pelvic floor dysfunction can show up in various and unexpected ways, including during bowel movements and even intercourse, which is why it’s key to find an expert with experience treating these issues (see sidebar).

Fortunately, the conversation around pelvic floor complications is evolving. “We’re starting to see patterns that might explain why you and I might have the same symptoms but maybe have different ways that we find resolutions,” says Pagliano. For runners, it might be a matter of your stride, your form, or even your breathing. “If someone holds their abdomen tight while they are running or are constantly holding their breath during normal everyday activities, we often see pelvic floor muscles that have higher tone or activity and actually don’t relax when they should. Sometimes this leads to leakage with running. Just strengthening the pelvic floor below won’t matter if those muscles are already ‘on’ and have lost the ability to contract and relax.”.

As for Gordon Garner, after finally finding the right therapist, he scaled back his running for a few weeks while working on stretching and breath-control exercises. In 2023, he ran 40 miles in a 24-hour period to celebrate his 40th birthday. “I was a little worried, just because I was testing these new boundaries, but with my exercises and my breathing techniques, I had no issues. I’m very in touch with my pelvic floor muscles now.”.

Liz finally found a therapist who helped her establish a strength-training routine in order to coordinate pelvic floor muscles again, pay attention to her body’s signals, and get back to running. Twenty months after giving birth, she raced her ninth marathon, without having to worry about leaking midrun. When your pelvic floor isn’t functioning as it should, “you realize that everything you do—breathing, talking, laughing, moving, carrying things—everything involves the pelvic floor,” Liz indicates.

With the right help and a better understanding of your body, pelvic floor problems can be solved. It’s a commitment, but your running will thank you. “Clients will always say, ‘Do I have to do these exercises forever?’” claims Reardon. “I tell them, ‘Yes, to some extent, if you’re going to keep running.’”.

Recent findings suggest that lauren Garges, DPT, director of pelvic rehab with St. Luke’s University Health Network in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, shares a simple at-home test that can help determine if you’re suffering from an overactive pelvic floor:.

It has been revealed that • Sit on a large stability ball or a rolled-up hand towel. There should be pressure on the perineum, the space between the genitals and anus.

It has been revealed that • Using the muscles you would use to stop the flow of urine or gas, imagine you’re trying to vacuum up a marble. Then, actively try to relax those muscles to see if they go back down, like an elevator.

“If they’re too tight, nothing may happen because your muscles are already as tight as they can get,” she notes. “Or you might be able to squeeze upward but cannot feel the downward [release]. That’s a sign of tension.”.

If you find contracting the muscles challenging, Garges indicates, it’s a sign of pelvic floor weakness.

In a recent development, before you start doing kegels—especially if you have incontinence or other pelvic floor problems—see a pelvic floor therapist to ensure it makes sense to add them to your routine, as they’re not for everyone, notes Nora Arnold, DPT, a pelvic health physical therapist with Johns Hopkins Medicine in Baltimore. If you get the go-ahead, Arnold offers these cues for correct form:.

• It’s best to get the hang of it lying down and then progressing to adding in practice sitting and standing.

• Squeeze your pelvic floor like you’re holding back from passing gas.

• Contract as if you’re stopping the flow of urine (but don’t do this while you’re actually peeing, as it could result in bladder infection).

• Draw your pubic bone and tailbone toward one another.

• Contract as if you are drawing your sit bones together.

• Pull your pelvic floor up as if lifting your bladder toward your heart.

Industry observers note that • You need to both squeeze and lift—people forget that second part. Make sure to fully relax the pelvic floor muscles between reps. Breathe through each contraction and relaxation.

• The number of repetitions is best decided by a PT; however, a good place to start is 3x10 contractions, holding for 10 seconds while breathing.

This deep breathing trains coordination between the pelvic floor and the diaphragm. When your diaphragm engages fully, it encourages your pelvic floor to relax and lengthen, Arnold notes.

• To start, lie on your back. You can also do this in child’s pose, happy baby pose, a deep squat, or reclined sitting.

• Breathe in through your nose for four counts. Let your breath be as slow and full as possible. Your pelvic floor should relax and lengthen passively, just like your belly.

• Exhale through your mouth for six counts.

Recent findings suggest that • For maximum benefit, try to incorporate this into your routine for five to 10 minutes a day. But even just 10 repetitions can make a difference.

Check experience / “As a runner, one of the most valuable things you can do is look for a pelvic floor therapist who knows sports medicine and pelvic health,” notes Julie W. Wiebe, DPT. If you’re postpartum, you might also seek out someone who has worked with moms; and if you’re male, you might look for a therapist who has experience with male clients. You can find a list of providers through the American Physical Therapy Association. Read online reviews to see what other patient experiences were like.

Consider a virtual visit / While some therapy sessions may need to be done in person, many can be done remotely. If there isn’t a great pelvic floor specialist in your area, try working with a therapist online. “I’ve been doing telehealth since before COVID-19,” indicates Carrie Pagliano, PT. “If I can get a really good sense of why you’re having symptoms by the questions that I ask, you can get resolution. The key is getting the right ‘why.’ After that, the ‘how’ is easy.” Make sure to offer details about whether you were a bedwetter as a child, your birthing history, or when you experience pelvic floor problems, for example.

Don’t stop until you find the right one / Garner, Quigley, and Liz all had to reach out to multiple practitioners before they found the right person. “You don’t try on one pair of pants, say they didn’t fit, and then never wear pants again,” indicates Reardon. “You have to keep trying different medical professionals until you find the right one.”.

She’s worked as an editor at Glamour, Essence, Seventeen, Heart & Soul, Parenting and more. She also co-edited ESSENCE’s The Black Woman’s Guide To Healthy Living. She received her B.A. in English from Harvard University, integrative health training at Duke, and plenty of life lessons in her hometown of Upcoming York City.

Industry News: Your First Gravel Ride Should Feel Like an Adventure—These 3 Tips Will Help You Enjoy It

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1481 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • The more riders I talk to, the more I see people switching over to gravel bikes.
  • Over the last few years, I’ve focused more on gravel riding than any other discipline of cycling.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

The more riders I talk to, the more I see people switching over to gravel bikes. I was leading a group ride for a shop in Newly introduced Jersey and the group primarily consisted of road cyclists on their first gravel ride. The line of the day was, “this is so fun—it’s like being a kid on a bike.” Gravel is challenging, but it’s also a different type of fun once you get off paved roads.

Over the last few years, I’ve focused more on gravel riding than any other discipline of cycling. My lunch rides typically end up being on the road and my strictly fun rides end up being on the mountain bike. But I’ve been gravitating more and more to the gravel bike because it can do a little bit of everything.

It has been revealed that I’ve taken gravel bikes on everything from 100-mile road rides with 10,000 feet of climbing to rides on singletrack trails where we should have been on a hardtail mountain bike at a minimum. On bikepacking routes, gravel day rides, and family rides towing my kids in their bike trailer, the gravel bike has been my go-to rig.

If you’re new to the sport, or even just getting into the category of gravel riding, it's easy to feel like there’s a mountain of knowledge needed as a barrier to entry. Here we’ll break down the top gravel tips you need to know to find success in those first few rides and beyond.

Sources indicate that when I ran a shop this was the first place I would start with folks who were gravel curious. The touchpoints on a bike are both where you contact the bike and where the bike touches the ground. The pieces of gear to focus on here are: chamois, gloves, saddle, bar tape, and tires.

The chamois and gloves are the first two because they are the parts on your body that touch the bike. I don’t like to use gloves that are overly padded, but I do like gloves that have a good level of tackiness to help with staying gripped to the handlebars. This year I’ve been using the Most Days Full Finger Gloves from Handup for everything from century gravel group rides to hard gravel rides with plenty of singletrack. The chamois can be a little more subjective, but I almost always suggest going with chamois bibs over chamois shorts.

Bibs stay in place better than shorts and this is especially notable from the movement you’re doing on a gravel ride. I’ve had plenty of people ask if they really need padded shorts for riding and the short answer is no. You can go riding with regular basketball shorts, but you’ll have a much better time riding with padded shorts or bibs. I like to compare it to riding a road bike on gravel. You can absolutely do that, and for a long time that’s what people did, but there’s a better way. My favorite pair are the Q36.5 Dottore Pro Bibs because they stay in place incredibly well and are comfortable from the first hour in the saddle to the 11th hour. The price point is a realistic hurdle for these Q36.5 bibs, but our Deputy Test Editor at Bicycling, Tara Seplavy, calls out this pair available on Amazon for just $40 in her roundup of cycling shorts.

Industry observers note that I personally like a tape that has some tackiness while also offering a bit of cushion for some dampening after miles of chattering gravel. My favorite tape is the Lizard Skin DSP Ultra Bar Tape. It comes in a range of colors and thicknesses, but I usually go with the 2.7mm or 3.5mm for people riding gravel. If you want a little extra comfort over the miles size up to the 3.5mm.

When it comes to saddles this is much more subjective because everyone’s sit bones are different and your preferred saddle can change depending on your position on the bike. Personally I have different saddles on each of my bikes based on how I use that specific bike. The biggest note on saddles is to avoid going with something super wide and overly padded. This can be a desirable thing to reach for after you’ve developed a bit of soreness from your initial rides, but try to avoid the beach cruiser type of saddles. These can cause extra friction and that’s the last thing you want to add to your gravel ride.

Finally, we get to where the bike touches the ground—the tires. When someone is looking to add comfort and versatility to a gravel bike I usually recommend bumping up the tire size. Most bikes don’t come stock with the widest tire you can fit on the bike, so check the technical specifications for your bike to see how wide you can go. Some of my favorite gravel tires are the Pirelli Cinturato H tires and the Continental Dubnital tires for their versatility on a range of terrains.

Industry observers note that this is a broad tip, but it is the most all-encompassing piece of advice I can give for gravel. Gravel riding burns more energy mile for mile and climb for climb compared to a road ride. Keep this in mind when you’re putting together your nutrition and hydration proposal as well as when you’re building the route. It’s vital to bring more calories than you think you need because you’ll likely be burning more calories compared to a road ride; it will take longer to get to the next refill stop compared to what you would expect, and those refuel spots are fewer and farther between on gravel roads and dirt trails compared to a road ride.

When it comes to setting up my route I always suggest riders have a way to navigate. When I got into gravel riding I used my phone for navigation with a handlebar mount on the bars. This worked initially, but because of the mud on some gravel routes, the possibility of falling, and how fast navigating on my phone killed the battery I quickly switched to a dedicated head unit. Head units that are capable of navigating reasonably well can range from a few hundred dollars to just shy of a thousand. At the moment I’m testing the COROS Dura 2 Solar and I love the fact that battery life can last for days of solid run time. A dedicated bike computer head unit is something that’s nice to have as you start to adventure, but if you currently have a smartwatch you can likely use that to navigate for now. It’s more convenient having the head unit in front of you for navigation compared to a smart watch. Lately I’ve been trying a few different watches from Garmin and COROS as a substitute for a bike computer and once I set up turn-by-turn notifications I’ve gotten used to navigating by the watch. Plus I can use the watch for other activities like runs, family hikes, and the occasional paddle.

According to recent reports, flat tires will eventually happen on a gravel ride. Step one is to bring a good flat kit with a reliable set of tire levers, a multitool (with a chain breaker), at least one tube, and a pump for inflation. I also typically bring a dollar bill as a backup for a tire boot in the event that I really blow out my tire. Ever since I had to use fallen leaves as a tire boot I always carry something to cover a large hole in the tire.

Step two is knowing how to use the tools you brought. Bringing a chain breaker tool or tire levers are great, but they won’t be much help if you aren’t able to figure out how to use them. When someone was buying a new bike from me I used to encourage them to practice taking the wheels off the bike, tires off the wheels, tubes out of the tires, then putting it all back together. Getting some laps on this process from the comfort of your home will make the process feel much smoother when you’re trying to finish the flat fix on the side of the trail.

A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

It has been revealed that my friend Sean Mullaney, the FI Tax Guy, recently published an interesting article about the potential downsides of annuities. One of his observations is so simple that I think it's easy to overlook:.

Industry observers note that most Americans already have an annuity. It's called Social Security.

It has been revealed that think about what an annuity is trying to accomplish. You give up some control over a pool of money in exchange for a predictable stream of income, often for the rest of your life. Social Security already provides lifetime income, with the added benefit of inflation adjustments.

For a married couple receiving substantial Social Security benefits, that could represent tens of thousands of dollars of annual income that they don't have to generate by selling investments.

Latest Update: I Break the Golden Rule of Running Every Race. You Should, Too

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

There’s an adage that most runners have heard at some point: “Nothing upcoming on race day.”.

In a recent development, it’s simple. You’re supposed to treat race day how you would your training runs, keeping things like your fueling, shoe choice, and routine similar. The time for experimenting is during the training block. On race day, there shouldn’t be any surprises that could throw you off.

Sources indicate that in my decade of competing, rarely has a race day gone to plan. I’ve lost track of the number of times I’ve been thrown off my routine by a traffic jam or a poor night of sleep. By expecting things to go perfectly, you’re almost setting yourself up for failure.

The key to race day, I’ve found, is to be adaptable.

In the spring of 2024, I signed up for the Brooklyn Half Marathon. I was going to run it as a workout to prepare for my first marathon later that fall.

It has been revealed that the day before the race was a disaster. My girlfriend and I drove into Brooklyn on Friday evening to pick up my bib at the expo. What is normally a 90-minute drive took much longer, and we barely made it to the pick-up before it closed. We were both tired and increasingly hangry, and the only thing nearby were some food trucks. So I cut my losses and stomached some greasy buffalo chicken mac and cheese. A far cry from my normal pre-race pasta dinner.

Surely this would come back to bite me, right?

According to recent reports, on race morning, things were equally as stressful. I made it to the start line with minutes to spare and not much time to properly warm up. And of course, the lines for the toilets were too long.

But as soon as the gun went off, I felt great. I was comfortable running at my marathon pace and finished with a lot of confidence for my full later in the year.

Industry observers note that the experience reinforced that, despite some hiccups, I would still be able to perform to my expectations. I would never plan to eat fast food or only get 5 hours of sleep, but I didn’t let it bother me too much. When “new” stuff pops up on race day, I take it in stride and move on.

According to recent reports, I also believe that there are some things you should intentionally keep latest on race day. The day of a race is special; it’s not supposed to be quotidian. Your adrenaline is higher because the stakes are higher, and channeling that energy can be impactful on your performance.

During my first marathon, I kept a few things special. I wore my favorite lightweight singlet that I sparingly wore during training to keep it pristine. I chose to race in a pair of Nike Alphaflys that I hardly wore during workouts to preserve the foam. I wore my favorite pair of socks and my favorite half tights and my favorite hat. Before driving to the start, I did a 10 minute walk at 5 a.m. at the recommendation of my coach—something I’d never done before—to get the blood flowing.

The idea of nothing latest on race day is, in my opinion, incompatible with the essence of race day.

Industry observers note that just look at my marathon. This was my debut at the distance. Everything about the experience was latest! The longest I had run was 18 miles, so I was venturing into uncharted territory.

Industry observers note that thankfully, the race went well. I used a significant negative split to hit my goal of sub 2:28, finishing in 2:27:05 for 29th place.

Sources indicate that sure, it’s key to keep some things similar to training. I kept my race fueling blueprint the same as my practice runs, and I was diligent about hitting my prescribed pace. But newness is the most exciting part of race day.

Industry observers note that race day is special and you should treat it as such. I hope the novelty never wears off.

Industry observers note that theo Kahler is the senior news editor at Runner’s World. He’s a former all-conference collegiate runner at Winthrop University, and he received his master’s degree in liberal arts studies from Wake Forest University, where he was a member of one of the top distance-running teams in the NCAA. Kahler has reported on the ground at major events such as the Paris Olympics, U.S. Olympic Trials, New York City Marathon, and Boston Marathon. He’s run 14:20 in the 5K, 1:05:37 in the half marathon, and finished 40th at the 2025 New York City Marathon. He enjoys spotting tracks from the sky on airplanes. (Look for colorful ovals around football fields.).

Isakova and Hidalgo Win Final WTCS Races in Abu Dhabi, Jorgensen Podiums

  • According to recent reports, 2025 world champion Lisa Tertsch (GER) was the big name going in, alongside Jeanne Lehair (LUX), who had been part of a sprint finish at the World Cup in Hong Kong the week before.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Wagner Araujo/World Triathlon).

According to recent reports, the postponed WTCS Abu Dhabi brought the World Triathlon Championship Series, as it is currently known, to a close ahead of its transition to T50 racing within the Triathlon World Tour. The sprint-distance showdown still attracted many of the sport’s top names, with Olympic qualification points and the chance to finish the season on a high and build momentum into 2027.

Recent findings suggest that the top spot on the podium was wide open in the women’s race, with the series’ undefeated champion Cassandre Beaugrand (FRA) absent. Add to the mix the shorter, sprint-distance format and hot, windy conditions set to play a factor, and it was anyone’s guess who would take it.

According to recent reports, 2025 world champion Lisa Tertsch (GER) was the big name going in, alongside Jeanne Lehair (LUX), who had been part of a sprint finish at the World Cup in Hong Kong the week before. However, Diana Isakova (RUS) was another athlete many had their eyes on after winning that sprint against Lehair and taking the World Cup win in Rome before that. American Gwen Jorgensen (USA) had shown glimmers of top form in recent races, placing fifth at WTCS Weihai and producing the second-fastest run split at the Grand Final in Pontevedra.

Into the warm, 82-degree water, three groups began to form near the front as the chop and currents made for one of the most difficult swims of the year.

According to recent reports, isakova and Lehair were among the first group out of the water, while Tertsch and Jorgensen exited more than 20 seconds behind. That deficit would rapidly balloon to over 30 seconds early on the bike, with another group between them and the front of the race.

Halfway through the bike, the front group of nine maintained its advantage as the third group swallowed the second to form one large chase pack. On such a tight, technical course, the larger group offered little additional benefit as the smaller pack ahead steadily increased its lead.

It has been revealed that at the end of the bike, Germany’s Laura Lindemann (GER) almost undid the work of the front, mishandling her bike after the dismount, almost causing a crash. Onto the run, a quick transition shot Isakova to the front, while around 36 seconds behind, Jorgensen and Tertsch were among the large group with significant work to do – and only 5km to do it.

In a recent development, by halfway, Isakova and Lehair were clear at the front, foreshadowing a repeat of the race in Hong Kong the week prior. Jorgensen remained 36 seconds behind but had gapped Tertsch and made her way into eighth place.

Recent findings suggest that that momentum continued for Jorgensen as suddenly eighth place became third and she could see the leaders up ahead. Unfortunately, the gap was just too large at that point. Isakova made her move with over 200 meters to go, picking up her first WTCS win and cementing her remarkable end to the year.

Lehair finished second and reflected that her efforts on the bike may have affected her run: “I may have used too much energy, but I am super happy with second place and my third podium of the year.”.

Jorgensen couldn’t believe her result, returning to the WTCS podium for the first time since 2016 at 40 years old and producing the fastest run split of the day.

“I thought I was out of this race but one of the coaches told me I was third and I couldn’t believe it,” she shared.

In the men’s race, this year’s Grand Final winner and sprint-distance specialist Matt Hauser (AUS) was wearing bib #1. With his prowess in the water, all eyes were on him in the absence of newly introduced world champion Vasco Vilaça (POR). Brazil’s Miguel Hidalgo (BRA), meanwhile, was looking to finally turn his training form into a result after some disappointing recent outings.

It has been revealed that upcoming Zealand’s Hayden Wilde (NZL) was the other substantial name on the lineup, having recently been approved to race both WTCS Abu Dhabi and Dubai T100. With the races falling within 24 hours of each other, that would not normally be allowed under World Triathlon rules. With his eyes firmly back on the Olympics, this was Wilde’s A-race for the weekend, according to New Zealand’s National Performance Manager Stephen Sheldrake.

Recent findings suggest that it started with a windy, choppy swim that mostly stayed compact until the return to the beach, when two lines formed toward the shore. One group, including Hauser, made a beeline for the beach to get out of the water as soon as possible and run along the shore toward transition. That worked well for the Australian, who entered T1 with a small gap over compatriot Luke Willian (AUS).

Recent findings suggest that wilde found himself 39 seconds in arrears, with work to do alongside recent Iquique World Cup winner David Cantero del Campo (ESP). They were in a large chase group aiming to gain time on the lead group of 11, but on such a short, fast, five-lap bike course, their work was cut out for them.

Recent findings suggest that almost immediately, however, the gap was nearly cut in half, with Wilde driving the chase to within 22 seconds by the end of the first lap. The pace was so hot that the group split apart, with only a few athletes able to go with him on the technical course.

Industry observers note that perhaps that woke up the front group, which managed to limit its losses over the remainder of the bike and reached T2 with around nine seconds on Wilde and organization. It was less than they would have hoped for against the stellar Kiwi runner, but the substantial question was whether the bike had stung his legs enough to hold him off. A slow transition from the 2025 winner of this race gave him even more work to do.

Industry observers note that onto the run, it didn’t take long for Hauser and Hidalgo to separate themselves at the front. Behind them, Wilde quickly recovered from his transition losses and moved through the rest of the front group alongside Shachar Sagiv (ISR).

The front two continued to push the pace and began adding time to Wilde behind. Hidalgo made his move before the second lap, and Hauser wasn’t able to respond. He promptly began to lose ground as the Brazilian looked comfortable all the way to the finish, taking the tape with an unmatched 14:20 5km.

In a recent development, it was a much-needed WTCS win to carry momentum into the 2027 Triathlon World Tour. Hauser shared afterward that he “could really feel the legs – and the whole year – in the back end of that race.”.

It has been revealed that wilde crossed the line in third, comfortably ahead of the rest of the field, but a 14:52 5km left him short of the run speed he is accustomed to producing in these races. He won’t have much time to digest the result, however, as he immediately has to travel to Dubai, where he would look to continue his dominant T100 season.

#114231. Industry News: We Tested 15 Electric Mini-Inflators. These Tiny Pumps Are Fast Enough to Replace CO₂ on Many Rides

📅 13 Nov 2025 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2275 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bicycling ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: We Tested 15 Electric Mini-Inflators. These Tiny Pumps Are Fast Enough to Replace CO₂ on Many Rides

📅 13 Nov 2025 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2275 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • According to recent reports, pumping up tires is a constant of cycling.
  • Some riders don’t worry about the exact psi in their tires, but others constantly check and analyze their air pressure, and the latter group may be onto something.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

According to recent reports, pumping up tires is a constant of cycling. Whether you’re checking pressure before a road ride, fixing a mid-ride flat on your gravel bike, fine-tuning your air pressure at the trailhead, or topping up tires on your kid’s bike in the garage, every cyclist needs to put air in their bike’s tires.

Some riders don’t worry about the exact psi in their tires, but others constantly check and analyze their air pressure, and the latter group may be onto something. In his story, “More Speed and Comfort? The Right Tire Pressure Can Give You Both,” Test Editor Dan Chabanov explains that having the correct pressure in your tires provides more confidence and control on rides.

Sources indicate that small, portable electric inflators have recently taken the cycling world by storm and quickly gained popularity with riders. For several decades, traditional pumps (floor, frame, and mini), CO₂ cartridges, and air compressors have been the go-to methods for filling tires. While mini-inflators don’t fully replace these other inflator types, these small electric units are now finding their way into riders’ toolboxes, gear bags, jersey pockets, and seat bags.

It has been revealed that over the last two seasons, we’ve subjected 15 electric mini-inflators to the same tests. We originally tested 11 inflators in 2025. In November 2026, we tested 4 models (from Cyclami, PDW, State, and Lezyne) and updated our Best Mini-Inflators ranking. A handful stand out for specific use cases or rider types. But these are only a few of the great pumps out there; choose the one that best fits your needs and budget.

According to recent reports, with svelte dimensions and a 106-gram weight, the Ultra Tiny is small enough to stash in a jersey pocket, flat kit, or bar bag. Plus, it quickly inflates tires of all sizes to pressure. The AS2’s super-accurate gauge also makes it worth considering for your home shop or carrying in a race-day tool kit. However, the pump runs a little hot.

At the media launch for the Colnago G-5X, someone asked the brand representatives if any inflators fit inside the internal frame storage. That led me to search for options that can fit inside frames. The Cyclami A5S came up in some discussions, so I ordered one on AliExpress to test.

Overall, it’s a solid little inflator that performs well—sub-one-minute inflation times and a 122-gram weight. The rounded profile and placement of the air chuck (on top rather than the side) help it squeeze into many frames’ internal storage doors. Of the five road, gravel, and mountain frames in the office I checked, the A5S fit into four (it didn’t fit into the Cervélo Caledonia).

Several Bicycling editors rely on the Air Rush on rides and at home. Overall, it’s a solid and dependable pick. It has a nice display, runs cool, and inflates road and gravel tires in under a minute. It also filled five road tires; that’s better than most units. I only wish it were slightly smaller for carrying in a seat bag or internal frame storage.

Like many RockBros products, this mini-inflator isn’t the best at any single thing, but it does everything pretty well overall. It gets tires up to pressure in under 50 seconds, doesn’t run too hot, isn’t too loud, and isn’t super heavy.

It has been revealed that the most expensive model in our test, the Ultimate, lived up to its name, hype, and steep price tag. And matching its durable appearance, this inflator is a beast—it gets tires up to pressure in under 30 seconds and inflates eight tires on a single charge. I tested Silca’s claim that the Ultimate will seat tubeless tires—surprisingly, it succeeded.

Industry observers note that the Ultimate was the quietest inflator in our testing and tied for the second-lowest temperature. Other than price, the biggest negatives are the Ultimate’s weight and size. One note: after almost a year of frequent use, an O-ring inside the pump failed. However, Silca offered to replace the unit under warranty.

According to recent reports, the Pocket SE doesn’t feature a display or gauge, but at only 90 grams, it weighs less than a single CO₂ cartridge and head. And though it takes roughly a minute to inflate a tire to full pressure, I can fill four tires on one charge. The Pocket SE’s one downside is that without a pressure gauge or a 72 psi cutoff, I’d be cautious using it on hookless tubeless road wheels.

For a year, I’ve carried the Pocket SE in my seat bag for flat fixes, and it has gotten me out of plenty of jams. My only complaint is that the button activates easily; a bump or pothole can trigger the unit if it isn’t carefully positioned in your bag.

According to recent reports, portland Design Works makes well-crafted, usable gear for everyday cyclists. The brand doesn’t take itself too seriously, and its products sometimes have whimsical or quirky elements (like its water bottle cages).

Industry observers note that PDW’s Essentials inflator follows this mold—it’s well-designed, looks good, and functions well. The Essentials inflates tires rapidly, and the gauge is pretty accurate. Its best feature is presets for different bike types (labeled road, gravel, mountain, and city). You can use these to set your tires for your quiver of bikes, or program them for different rides, wheelsets, or riders in your house.

Sources indicate that the screw-on chuck is slightly tricky to use and leaks some air if not fastened correctly. While the unit’s body doesn’t run hot, the hose’s base certainly does: heed that yellow warning tag.

According to recent reports, mini-inflators are pint-sized electric air compressors. Larger electric pumps have been around for many years and are commonly used at home, in the garage, or the workshop. Some people carry electric pumps in their vehicles to air up car or truck tires and fill inflatable rafts or SUPs. Cordless air inflators have been a common sight around World Cup mountain bike team paddocks and cyclocross pit zones for several years.

Yet cyclists only started using these inflators within the last three years, when the prices dropped, the form factor shrank, and battery life increased. Riders soon found electric inflators perfect for the garage or the trailhead. Plus, their smaller size makes them much easier to toss in a bike bag or luggage than a floor pump when flying with a bike.

In a recent development, several cycling equipment brands have released models tailored to bicycle riders’ tastes and preferences. Some companies have even cut enough weight and reduced the proportions to make electric mini-inflators a viable option for carrying in a jersey pocket or flat kit on rides.

The current crop of bike-specific mini-inflators can be broken down into two groups:.

1) Small enough to bring on a ride, and 2) Everything else.

According to recent reports, of course, your definition of “small enough” might vary greatly from another cyclist’s. If you ride with a bar bag or frame pack, an inflator like the Portland Design Works Essentials or Trek Air Rush might be sufficiently tiny. However, if you carry everything in a ride wallet or obsess about weight, even Silca’s 112-gram Elettrico Micro might be too large for you.

For our testing, we focused on mini-inflators sold by cycling-specific brands and ones marketed for bicycle use. This isn’t an exhaustive test of every inflator available; instead, it provides context to help you choose one best for your needs.

In two years of testing, we’ve evaluated fifteen models across a wide price range ($15 to $160). These include mini-inflators from respected cycling brands, options from smaller companies, and those that fly under the radar.

Industry observers note that to test if size matters, I picked some based on their tidy proportions and low weight. I also chose a couple of larger, heavier options to see whether they push air significantly faster or fill more tires than other mini-inflators. I also bought the cheapest mini-inflator available on Amazon ($14.90 on the day I was shopping) to test it against the pack and see if spending more on a pump really matters.

Sources indicate that as with other Bicycling head-to-head product tests (like insulated water bottles, flared handlebars, and wide road tires), we evaluated electric mini-inflators based on real-world requirements, not intricate lab tests. Riders can replicate at home without much fancy equipment.

We inflated the tires to air pressures for a 180-pound cyclist riding a road, gravel, and mountain bike in average conditions (as recommended by Wolf Tooth’s app). For road riders, we recorded the time to inflate a 28mm-wide tubeless tire to 65 psi. We also measured the time to reach 30 psi on a 45mm gravel tire. For mountain bike riders (or folks riding fresh-school gravel bikes), we clocked the time to 20 psi on a 29x2.3-inch tire. To evaluate the pumps without built-in gauges, we measured the pressure they reached after 50 seconds.

After timing inflation speeds for each category, I fully recharged all devices. The next morning, I tested how many times each electric mini-inflator could fill a 28mm road tire to 65 psi from fully flat. To prevent overheating, I let each inflator cool down for ten minutes between fills.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to real-world tests, we also measured three common concerns of electric pump buyers: Temperature, noise, and gauge accuracy. For these tests, I borrowed equipment from my colleagues on the Popular Mechanics test team.

According to recent reports, this included a specially designed fixture that measures bike pump gauge accuracy. Gauge accuracy is important, especially for riders using hookless tubeless road wheels. Since the maximum allowed pressure for these wheel systems under ETRTO standards is 5 bar (72.5 psi), you don’t want to risk a tire blowing off a rim due to a wildly inaccurate pump reading.

Like other users, I have personally experienced noise and heat build-up problems with electric mini-inflators. Early one morning at Sea Otter Classic, my inflator woke the cyclist in the hotel room next door—my sincere apologies to him! Later, on an All Bodies on Bikes group ride, the inflator I borrowed from another cyclist to change a flat melted the plastic valve of my spare TPU tube.

Lesson Learned: Due to excess heat, always use an extension hose when filling plastic-valved tubes with an electric mini-pump.

According to recent reports, “Do I proposal to carry this on rides?” you ask when purchasing a mini-inflator. If you answered “yes”, look for lighter-weight and smaller-profile models. If you only plan to use the inflator at home, at the trailhead, or at races, don’t focus on size or weight.

Industry observers note that unless you only need to get out of a jam on the side of a road or trail, look for models that fill more than two tires. This allows you to adjust tire pressure and inflate tires on other bikes or spare wheels (and for friends to borrow before a ride—because you know they will need it).

After evaluating these mini-inflators, my key takeaway is that price doesn’t exactly make it the best for your needs. The most expensive pump in our test has brilliant inflation speed, is the quietest, and doesn’t run hot—plus it fills lots of tires. But it’s too heavy and large for most cyclists to carry on rides. However, spending more doesn’t guarantee better performance either, as some pricier models didn’t outshine the low- or mid-priced models. And, as I found out from testing, you probably don’t want to buy the absolute cheapest possible option either (luckily, this model is no longer available).

Skimming listings for different devices, you’ll notice (from similar design details and parts) that a select few vendors manufacture many electric inflator models for every brand. But even if a mini-inflator shares the same outer silicone protector, case, buttons, or display, it doesn’t mean they’re identical. For example, in our testing, the Rockbros model outperformed the extremely similar-looking Muc-Off Air Mach pump.

Unless you specifically need a lightweight, compact mini-inflator for on-the-bike use, spend a little more for a model with a built-in gauge. A display is super handy, and you can pre-set your desired pressure within 1 psi (some even read to tenths).

Recent findings suggest that pro Tip: If you buy an inflator without a built-in gauge, time how long it takes to reach your optimal ride pressure from fully flat before bringing it out on the road or trail. Then, when you’re airing up a flat fix, you can count off (or use a timer) to get you relatively close to your riding pressure.

Industry observers note that as Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and Upcoming England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

New runners always ask me, “What’s the best running shoe?” But there’s truly not one trainer that outperforms them all. Instead of recommending one single shoe, I consider the runner’s experience level and what they’re training for.

Industry observers note that maybe you signed up for your first 5K or you’re a more experienced runner setting your sights on training for your first marathon. Or maybe you’re trying to get faster or just want a new pair of kicks to start run/walking. From beginner to vet, road to trail, neutral to stability, there’s a shoe out there for everyone.

Sources indicate that men kind of have the upper hand in terms of running shoes because most models are designed for men’s feet by default. Even on unisex racing shoes, runners with smaller ankles (typically women) often need to use special tricks like the heel lock lacing technique to tighten the fit because they were built based on a men’s last with a wider collar.

Recent findings suggest that that doesn’t mean you can zone out when it comes to finding the best fit. We have a handy guide to help you find your approximate size before shopping. There’s also width to consider, as well as intention: Do you want a grippy, durable trail shoe or a lightweight trainer for tempo runs?

Here, we break it down for you by naming our top 10 running shoes for men and provide guidance on what features you should consider.

Looking for a solid daily trainer → Nike Pegasus 42Searching for a mileage monster → Newly introduced Balance EllipseA new runner → Brooks Ghost 18Adding speedwork → Adidas Adizero Evo SLA run/walker → On Cloudmonster 3An overpronator → Saucony Guide 19Injury-prone → Saucony Triumph 24Needing a wider fit → Hoka Clifton 11Racing a marathon → Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 5Hitting the trailhead → Altra Experience Wild 3.

In a recent development, I’ve chosen to highlight each of these shoes based on feedback from the men on our editorial team, as well as the Runner’s World wear-tester program. We frequently update the lineup to ensure we're giving you the best, most up-to-date recommendations for every type of run—and runner.

Please note: While we’re experts at vetting the best footwear and patch these lists often, retailer prices and stock fluctuate constantly. Our recommendations may not always be available in a given size or color. We’ll do our best to update our links to make sure you can get every pick as often as possible.

The Peg is back—and our testing proves it was worth the wait. The newest iteration is snappier and more responsive, thanks to a full-length Air Zoom unit that had one tester say, “the design leans into speed.” The shoe is a major improvement compared to its predecessor, which wasn’t necessarily bad; the Peg 41’s ride was just a little lackluster according to our testers’ feedback.

Industry observers note that nike stepped in to make sure the Pegasus 42 would have more rebound. The last is also modified to accommodate wider feet.

It has been revealed that “The Nike Pegasus 42 is a solid and stable everyday trainer. Back in 1990 when I was running cross country in high school, my very first shoe was the Nike Air Pegasus and they have made some excellent changes over the past 35 years,” said tester Steven Blasi.

“The Pegasus 42 is nothing like my Pegasus from my high school days,” he continued. “The shoe is not too hard, not too soft, it is just right. The slight rocker bottom of the shoe made for a nice and smooth transition from heel to forefoot and the [Air Zoom unit] added the extra push.”.

According to recent reports, with the Ellipse you get an affordable model that packs incredible comfort and bounce. Upcoming Balance Senior Global Project Manager Paul Zielinski explained to Runner’s World how the brand set out to capture the communal aspect of our sport in a shoe. Think of the Ellipse as your “running group model,” the shoe’s ride meant to embody the rush of going on a fun run with friends.

The shoe has a retooled version of the brand’s Fresh Foam X; it has new geometry to make it springier. Though the shoe feels slightly bulky—it’s not intended for speedwork—its midsole produces a trampoline-like bounce that energizes your run.

According to recent reports, “I like the foam,” remarked shoe tester and Director of News Andrew Daniels. “Some of the shoes I ran in most recently feel more firm than these, like a gym mat. This isn’t *super* sponge-y, but more in that sweet spot of just-right firm and just-right squishy, where it stays pretty bouncy for most of the run and provides good cushioning on the landings.”.

Our men and women testers were split on the Ghost 18. Men liked the shoe’s ride and comfy fit, saying that even though the foam isn’t as responsive as other daily trainers they’ve tested, the Ghost 18 is a reliable shoe for logging easy workouts.

According to recent reports, “[The Ghost 18] is well-cushioned, especially in the heel,” noted Photo Director John Hamilton. “Really noticed it on a long downhill at the end of a longer run. The foam was supportive and adequate especially for slower paces but lacked a ‘pop’ when picking up the pace.”.

Hamilton also noted the toe area felt slightly narrow and that a wider width would remedy this hitch (the shoe is available in wide and extra wide, as well as narrow widths).

It has been revealed that on the other end, the air mesh upper was uncomfortable for our women testers, who complained they got hot spots under the big toe area. It’s funny to say an iteration of a shoe works better for men’s feet, but that seems to be the case with our testing—which is why the Ghost 18 made this list as Best Daily Trainer.

Sources indicate that “I really like easy cruising, when I lay back on my heel and float,” remarked Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate. “I think that’s where this shoe works best, and probably why it’s going to work for newer runners and the majority of us who heel strike.”.

Sources indicate that dengate noted in February 2025 that the Adizero Evo SL was the shoe of the year, and that he’d feast on it if something better came along. What would lead him to make such a bold claim? For starters, the Lightstrike Pro foam in its midsole is the same cushioning Adidas used in its incredibly effective competition-grade marathon shoe, the Adios Pro 4. The Evo SL drops the Pro 4’s carbon-fiber plate in favor of a nylon shank, lending stability in a more affordable way. Because of its best value attributes (you get a heckuva lot for just $150) and dynamic construction, the shoe has been a mainstay on our lists. Dengate is definitely saved from snacking on shoelaces.

The shoe has some minor drawbacks: The tongue tends to go askew mid-run, and the fit was narrow for some of our testers. These were, by the testers’ admissions, pet peeves, though. They all said they’d continue running in the shoe, especially for speedy efforts.

Industry observers note that “I like the lightweight feel of these sneakers,” stated tester Ahmad Norman. “This helps me glide and turnover my stride at a rapid pace. I can see that training in these sneakers will most certainly increase my tempo and bring down my splits per mile.”.

We love the Cloudmonster 3 at any pace, from casual walks to 4:30 strides. Our testers were impressed with the firm—but soft—Helion cushioning that provided a responsive ride for almost any kind of effort.

The shoe has On’s triple-layer CloudTec cushioning, which makes the bounce and support not much of a mystery when you see the system of holes on the shoe’s rocker shape. A Speedboard promotes propulsion and smooth push-off.

According to recent reports, “When I slid my foot into these shoes to try on at the pickup I was instantly blown away with the shear joy it was to have these shoes on my feet,” stated shoe tester Dave Brattley. “Needless to say there were some high expectations for them to perform just as well during run and they didn’t disappoint! Fit and feel, check, forefoot cushioning that’s soft but you can still feel the road, check, heel cushioning while walking, check, and durability, check! There wasn’t anything that felt off about these shoes.”.

According to recent reports, the Guide 19 is basically the same—thank goodness!—as its predecessor. It features the brand’s CenterPath technology, which adds a broader base and higher sidewalls to create a more cradled fit that provides support without constriction. Wide-footed testers love how this feature also creates an accommodating fit in the midfoot.

It has been revealed that pwrrun foam provides max-cushioning, making the shoe suitable for long runs and recovery days. The shoe’s rocker profile promotes fast turnover.

“Like its predecessor, this shoe made me feel good before even starting my runs,” remarked tester Dave Block. “I just love the comfort and feel! The shoe is very soft and slips on easily. I can’t think of any other shoe that feels this great, with the possible exception of the Adidas Pureboost, but that’s going back several years.”.

The Triumph 24 is a true triumph for Saucony. The max-cushioned shoe is a mere 8.8 ounces in a men’s size 9. That’s lighter than our favorite daily trainer, the Ghost 18. The shoe’s new IncrediLux foam provides an incredibly soft—but supportive—platform.

The foam also delivers high rebound, resulting in runs that start off slow then gradually go uptempo because of the shoe’s blend of comfort and high energy return.

Testers loved the fit and feel of the trainer. For runner Phil Nicolosi, it was all about the journey and not about the stats on his watch.

“I rated the Saucony Triumph 24 very highly overall because it was one of the most comfortable max-cushioned shoes I have worn,” he remarked. “The fit was excellent, the upper was comfortable, and the cushioning made it easy on my aging body. It was especially good for scenic, easy runs when I was not worried about pace and just wanted to enjoy being out there.”.

Industry observers note that the Clifton is the epitome of a Hoka trainer: soft and supportive cushioning; padded, comfy, accommodating upper; rocker geometry that smooths heel-to-toe transitions. Known for its max-cushioned models, Hoka released two Cliftons this year. The Clifton Pro is an amped-up version of the Clifton 11. But in terms of recommending the best men’s shoes, I’m sticking with the original Clifton.

The Clifton 11 is like running with an old friend. The daily trainer’s rep is up there with the Nike Peg and Brooks Ghost for its overall comfort and responsive ride. The shoe has a compression-molded EVA midsole (CMEVA). Even though it’s comparatively not as bouncy as other trainers with superior foams, you still get high-energy return for daily miles and excellent support running long. It’s also a favorite for run/walking.

Hoka Clifton 11 Running Review | Hoka Clifton 11 Walking Review.

The shoe worn by the fastest man, Sabastian Sawe, was the Adidas Adios Pro Evo 3. That shoe sold out in record time—at a pretty penny for $500. The next best thing? The Adidas Adios Pro 5, which is about half the price and in stock now.

Sources indicate that the Pro 5 features a upcoming carbon form in the shoe’s midsole; in place of rods, which mapped out the pad of your foot like your metatarsals, Adidas introduces a carbon rim. According to the brand, the rim results in 12.5 percent weight savings. Our testers found the new tech even more explosive than the Pro 4. The ride is snappy and delivers an aggressive but stable bounce thanks to the updated Lightstrike Pro foam, which is slightly firmer.

Industry observers note that dengate praised the shoe’s performance during a speed workout—even though he got dropped. “I loved that I could feel the foam compress and load up with each footstrike, yet feel bouncy and responsive at toe-off,” he mentioned. “These shoes wanted more than my legs could give.”.

Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 5 Review.

The Experience Wild 3 has supportive cushioning without limiting ground feel, 3.5mm lugs that bite into loose terrain, and a comfortable, accommodating fit that allows you to splay your toes when hitting the trail.

Sources indicate that with a 4mm drop, it’s a good option for runners not ready to commit to zero-drop but who still want to dabble in low-drop. The upper has a protective toe sweep and gaiter attachments.

“[The Experience Wild 3] takes the shoe to the next level with a redesigned upper that fits more generously but doesn’t make you feel like you are swimming around, plusher cushioning that absorbs firmer ground yet remains stable, and a lug pattern on the MaxTrac outsole that I felt was superior to each of the previous models in terms of grip,” stated tester John Mikovits.

The shoe is also available with a Vibram Megagrip outsole.

Recent findings suggest that fit and comfort go hand-in-hand. You don’t want to constantly think of how loose or tight your shoes feel as you run. We recommend looking for a thumbnail’s width of toe room between the tip of your longest toe and the nose of the shoe, which leaves space for your feet to swell as you run.

Recent findings suggest that generally speaking, your running shoe should be a half size up compared to your regular street shoes. When in doubt, I generally recommend going in for a fitting and getting expert help so you're sure you find your perfect size.

Be mindful of heel rubbing and slipping. You can use the heel lock lacing technique for a snugger fit around the collar. Some runners have a high instep as well. If you feel pressure in the lacing area, you may need a shoe with a wider width.

Recent findings suggest that it’s normal to have some pronation as you run. If your foot rolls excessively inward, however, you may be susceptible to knee and lower back injuries. See a specialist, like a podiatrist or physical therapist, for a gait evaluation. Special insoles and shoes with medial posts can help severe overpronators with erratic foot rolling.

If you have mild pronation or late-onset pronation, some stability shoes have holistic features, like guide rails, that act as subtle bumpers to help you when your form gets sloppy.

According to recent reports, we recommend the Brooks Ghost 18 for beginner runners because it provides Goldilocks cushioning: not too soft, nor too hard. It’s a great starting point to see if you sway firm and lightweight or soft and max-cushioned.

Recent findings suggest that runners prefer lightweight shoes with a thinner midsole for faster efforts. These past years, however, have proven you don’t have to sacrifice stack height for speed thanks to the arrival of super foams. Still, some runners may prefer a simpler, more grounded lightweight racing flat for track workouts or hard tempos.

Max-cushioned trainers are great for long runs and recovery runs postrace, when you’re gradually adding miles again after taking time off from running.

Why should I pay more than $200 for a pair of running shoes?

Top-of-the-line running shoes made for competition feature premium materials, which generally force their prices well over the $200 line. Super foams enhance the running experience; paired with a carbon-fiber plate, this combination can improve your running economy.

These shoes are an investment and a novelty. Not everyone will experience a “4 percent” improvement. And even though super shoes eight years later are made of more durable materials (the recommended usage used to be 100 miles per pair), shelf life is still dependent on the wearer and their wear pattern.

You can also find top quality shoes for a lesser price. Training shoes, like the Saucony Endorphin Speed 6, are constructed with premium foams and have a much lower price tag than their carbon-fiber counterparts.

Can a running shoe actually make me faster?

Recent findings suggest that when Nike released the original Vaporfly in 2017, many runners misinterpreted the brand's “4 percent” claim to mean running 4 percent faster, rather than improving energy efficiency. The combination of responsive super foam with a carbon-fiber plate to work as a stabilizer (the plate actually works in tandem with the foam and isn’t the root cause for propulsion) helps the wearer run more efficiently, using less oxygen and less energy to maintain their speed.

Regardless of what a brand claims, though, the only universal truth about a shoe’s impact on running performance is that no two runners will see the same benefits. A shoe is a tool: It can help you train to become stronger and improve your stride. Lightweight shoes with responsive foams can make you feel swifter and deliver more rebound, but you are the one getting faster.

Amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.
