Physical Therapists Share the Most Effective QL Stretches and Exercises for Runners With Lower Back and Hip Pain

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1200 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most runners are familiar with the significant muscles involved in running, such as the quads, hamstrings, and glutes.
  • Industry observers note that A deep trunk muscle, the QL attaches to the lower spine and the back side of the pelvis, Nicole Haas, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and founder of Boulder Physiolab in Colorado, tells Runner’s World.
  • It has been revealed that when you run, the QL plays more of a stabilizing role, working to control your pelvis and trunk while you stride, states Spencer Agnew, PT, DPT, a physical therapist at Sword Health and run coach with Wisconsin-based Ascent Endurance Group.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most runners are familiar with the significant muscles involved in running, such as the quads, hamstrings, and glutes. But there are lesser-known—yet still important—players that can influence running performance. One example: the quadratus lumborum, or QL for short.

Industry observers note that A deep trunk muscle, the QL attaches to the lower spine and the back side of the pelvis, Nicole Haas, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and founder of Boulder Physiolab in Colorado, tells Runner’s World. It serves a few different functions in daily life, such as helping you arch your back, bend to the side, and rotate your upper body, Haas explains.

It has been revealed that when you run, the QL plays more of a stabilizing role, working to control your pelvis and trunk while you stride, states Spencer Agnew, PT, DPT, a physical therapist at Sword Health and run coach with Wisconsin-based Ascent Endurance Group. The QL also assists with breathing, specifically when you inhale, Agnew adds.

It has been revealed that if this muscle is tight or irritated, you’ll likely feel pain in your back or sacroiliac joints, which link the pelvis and lower spine, Agnew claims. To help you avoid these aches, we asked the PTs to explain what can cause an angry QL and how to relieve it.

In a recent development, there are several reasons your QL might be yelling at you. A common one? Your hip flexors are tight. In particular, when the psoas (a massive, rope-like hip flexor muscle that runs from your lower back to the front of your hip) is shortened, it can pull your pelvis into an anterior tilt, meaning your pelvis is tipped forward, arching your lower back. In many cases, this yanks on your QL as well, because the psoas and QL both insert into the same group of vertebrae in your lower back, Agnew explains.

Industry observers note that another culprit is weak glutes. When your glutes aren’t strong enough to help you maintain good running mechanics, your knee can collapse inward as you land and your opposite-side hip can dip down, Haas explains. This, in turn, can cause your trunk to side bend and rotate, thus placing more strain on your QL over time. Running downhill can exacerbate the problem, Haas adds, because that can cause your lower back to arch and place further stress on your QL.

Yet another cause of an irritated QL is upper-back stiffness. Restrictions in the upper part of the spine can shift more workload onto the QL, Haas explains. So can complications in your shoulders, hips, and mid-back. If these areas aren’t moving like they should due to pain or injury, your QL may receive added stress, Haas claims.

It has been revealed that keep in mind that in some cases, your QL may hurt because it’s taking on a bunch of extra stress it’s not meant to, but the muscle itself probably isn’t tight. “It’s more like your QL is just irritated because everything has been collapsing around it and loading it,” Haas indicates. “It’s overworked and underappreciated.”.

According to recent reports, A tight-feeling QL is worth addressing because it can lead to a few not-so-great complications if left unchecked. A big one? Compromised running mechanics.

Recent findings suggest that A tight QL, as mentioned, can shorten your hip flexors and pull your pelvis into an anterior tilt, which will reduce your knee lift as you stride, Agnew claims. As a result, “you’re not going to be able to generate as much force moving forward, and you’ll have more of an arched-back position when you run,” he explains. In many cases, this can deliver a double whammy of reduced performance and increased back pain, he says.

Recent findings suggest that on top of that, a tight QL can also hinder your breathing. As mentioned above, one of the QL’s jobs is to help you inhale, so when this muscle is tight, you may not be able to breathe as deeply or easily, Agnew claims.

Recent findings suggest that plagued by what you think may be an irritated QL? Try Agnew’s three-step at-home series to help reduce your discomfort.

Industry observers note that perform this sequence as often as every day if you’re in significant discomfort that’s limiting your ability to run. In the case of minor pain, incorporate this series two to three times per week. On the days you run, perform the myofascial release, pelvic tilts, and hip hikes before you lace up, then tackle the other components afterward.

This can help turn down the pain response in a barking QL by desensitizing soft tissue, Agnew explains.

How to Perform Myofascial Release.

The pelvic tilts help you learn how to coordinate and control pelvic motion so you can maintain proper mechanics while running, and the hip hikes help activate your QL. The kettlebell side bend increases blood flow to the muscle, which can aid in healing. Finally, the suitcase carry increases strength, stability, and engagement of the muscle, which can ensure it functions properly during a run.

Lengthen your QL—as well as tight hip flexors—with this two-for-one half-kneeling lunge stretch.

Recent findings suggest that do these moves daily or several times per day to mobilize your lower back. Perform them before or after a run. Important caveat: If your QL hurts more after stretching—or if your QL pain returns soon after stretching—then stretches are likely not the solution and you should stop doing them, Haas explains.

Dynamic QL Mobility + Hip 90/90.

Recent findings suggest that to start, do one set of these moves daily to help your body learn the neuromuscular patterns. (The caveat: If you feel sore, then skip a day.) After about six weeks, do these moves two to three times per week as part of your regular strength-training routine.

This exercise targets the glutes and works on pelvic control in a movement pattern that’s similar to running. Think of it as an opportunity to train proper glute use in your running form, which will help unload any strain on your QL caused by weak glutes.

This exercise can improve core stability and strengthen the glutes, resulting in improved running mechanics and less stress on your QL. You’ll need a long, looped resistance band.

Sometimes, despite your best at-home efforts to treat an irritated QL, it’s still best to get checked out by a physical therapist. Haas recommends booking a PT appointment if you try the above stretches and strength moves and don’t see improvements after about two weeks.

Agnew suggests getting evaluated by a PT if you’re in so much pain that it’s inhibiting your running. In this case, getting seen sooner can help mitigate pain before further issues arise, Agnew explains.

Latest Update: Here’s What to Know About the Nike Vaporfly 5

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (879 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article.
  • Sources indicate that nike unveiled a whole slate of innovations it has in the works, including a fresh method for creating Air units, the return of the Nike Free, and a look at the future of its sportswear.
  • Recent findings suggest that the substantial highlight is that the road racing shoe is basically going to have a “spring” in it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that nike unveiled a whole slate of innovations it has in the works, including a fresh method for creating Air units, the return of the Nike Free, and a look at the future of its sportswear. But the most interesting product unveiling is the Vaporfly 5—Nike is calling it the “most aggressive Vaporfly yet.”.

Recent findings suggest that the substantial highlight is that the road racing shoe is basically going to have a “spring” in it. “At the center of Vaporfly 5 is a new, wave-shaped Flyplate,” Nike’s announcement read. “A ripple through the midfoot creates a spring-like sensation under the arch.”.

I got a look at the prototype in Chicago last month, when I visited Nike’s headquarters during marathon weekend. There, I asked Bret Schoolmeester, vice president of running footwear product, if he was concerned about calling the shoe a spring. He is not, and told me that shoes basically serve as springs already given the bouncy modern foams being used.

In a recent development, remember back to the first carbon-plated shoes, when much of the uproar around them was because people believed the plates would act like springs. That’s not really what came to fruition, as we found that the plates basically were used as stiffening mechanisms to create leverage.

World Athletics rules permit a plate in a single layer, and that’s what Nike is technically creating here. The difference is in the shaping. The bump in this latest plate, combined with the midsole geometry, will allow the plate to flex when you land and snap back to shape to propel you ahead.

Nike also looked at ways to strip weight, which you can see through the big carve-outs in the foam, the super thin Vapor Mesh upper, and sparse use of Goatek outsole. Another weight-saving measure is adding ZoomX LT, the lightweight version of ZoomX that we saw in the Alphafly 4. A thin layer of that sits between the plate and your foot, while the standard ZoomX is used between the plate and the road for control and responsiveness.

Recent findings suggest that with these changes, Nike is positioning this shoe to be a shorter-distance road racing shoe. Given the overhaul of the Alphafly 4 and the announcement of the Apex, a hyper shoe designed for elite marathoners, the Vaporfly is being pitched for races up to 13.1 miles. Sure, some runners will lace it up for a full marathon, though it’s going to be lighter and snappier to excel at faster speeds.

The shoe won’t be available until “fall 2027,” but Nike is showing it off early as it drums up excitement for upcoming footwear and apparel at its World of Athletes event.

Beyond the Vaporfly 5, there were some other cool new innovations revealed, including “Tuned Air.” Through a new manufacturing process, Nike is able to create lighter Air units more swiftly, which can be customized for various applications.

I spoke with Phil McCartney, executive vice president, chief innovation, design and product officer, last week about Tuned Air. He explained that through a proprietary digital print and selective lamination process, Air units can be created with different amounts of cushioning and support. Those characteristics are delivered not only through the physical geometries of the Air unit, but also by varying the pressure within each unit.

Recent findings suggest that nike has previously talked about “Tuned Air,” and we saw it in use with the Pegasus Plus 2. But that was really just offering a few different air bags. The idea is that bigger shoes are worn by bigger runners and, thus, bigger Air units with greater gas pressures are required. So, shoes any smaller than a women’s 7.5 (M6) got an Air unit that’s 9.5 mm thick with 15 psi. Moving on up to a men’s 10.5 (W12), the bag gains 2 mm thickness. And, those runners with larger feet sit atop the 11.5mm-thick unit pumped up with 20 psi.

In a recent development, these new units, however, are different altogether. Nike found a way to remove the need for pins and rigid zones that formed the Air units, so that each can offer better cushioning and responsiveness.

Like the Vaporfly 5, Tuned Air won’t make an appearance until later in 2027. The prototype shoe teased in the image above has one massive Air unit making up the entire midsole. No word yet on which model or franchise that shoe will reside.

While we wait, the fastest Nike available to any of us remains the Alphafly 4.

Jeff is Runner-in-Chief for Runner’s World and the director of product testing. He has tested and reviewed running shoes, GPS watches, headphones, apparel, and more for nearly two decades. He regularly tests more than 100 pairs of shoes each year, and once had a 257-day streak running in different models. Jeff can usually be found on the roads, racing anything from the mile to a marathon, but he also enjoys racing up mountains and on snowshoes. When he’s not running, you’ll probably find him hanging from a ladder making repairs and renovations to his house (he’s also director of product testing for Popular Mechanics).

Business Class Product Worldwide.

According to recent reports, picture this: you're seated in a private suite at 38,000 feet somewhere over the Atlantic, your door clicked shut behind you, a glass of Dom Pérignon on the side table, and a fully flat bed dressed in Westin Heavenly bedding waiting for you. Your partner is in the suite next to yours — and when you lower the center dividing panel, you're sharing a meal in what Qatar Airways calls the "Double Bed" configuration. This is QSuites, and it is, without exaggeration, the single most celebrated business class product in the world. Now here's the number that stops the ChooseFI community cold: a cash ticket in QSuites from New York JFK to Doha DOH typically runs **$5,000 to $10,000 per person**. That's a mortgage payment. That's a family vacation budget. That's real money that compounds in an index fund. With Qatar Avios through the Privilege Club program, that same seat costs **75,000 Avios**. When you do the math against even the conservative cash price of $5,000, you're extracting **6.7 cents per point**. Against the top-end cash price of $10,000, that's **13.3 cents per point** — in a world where most loyalty currencies are "worth" 1 cent each. This is a 6x to 13x multiplier on every point you've earned. Here's what makes this a genuine pricing inefficiency rather than just marketing: Qatar's award chart is fixed and partner-friendly, meaning the number of points required doesn't scale dynamically with cash prices the way most airline programs now do. When demand spikes and cash fares hit $10,000, your award price stays exactly 75,000 Avios. The loyalty program hasn't caught up to the revenue management engine, and that gap is your opportunity. For anyone on the path to financial independence, this is the travel rewards philosophy in its purest form: redirect real spending you're already doing onto the right cards, accumulate points as a byproduct, and convert those points into experiences that would otherwise require liquidating investments. The QSuites redemption is the pinnacle of that system — a **nearly free** business class experience that delivers more luxury per point than almost anything else in the world of travel rewards.

The mechanism behind this sweet spot is elegant once you see it, and once you see it, you'll start recognizing similar patterns everywhere in the loyalty space.

Qatar prices its own flights in its own currency — and that currency is cheap to acquire.

Sources indicate that qatar Airways Privilege Club Avios are the program's native points currency. When Qatar sets award prices for its own operated flights, including QSuites, it prices them in a way that's competitive and fixed — not subject to the dynamic pricing algorithms that have made programs like United MileagePlus or Delta SkyMiles increasingly unpredictable. Seventy-five thousand Avios for a transatlantic or transoceanic business class seat is a published, stable price. Qatar isn't trying to extract maximum value from every award booking; they want to keep the program attractive to drive loyalty.

The critical insight is this: you don't need to earn Qatar Avios through Qatar flights. You can transfer them directly from credit card programs you're probably already using.

Citi ThankYou Points → Qatar Avios at 1:1 — This is the fastest and cleanest route. Transfers from Citi to Qatar are instant, meaning you can search for availability, confirm the seat is bookable, and transfer in the same session without risk. For anyone holding a Citi Premier or Citi Prestige card, this is a direct pipeline to QSuites.

Capital One Miles → Qatar Avios at 1:1 — A strong secondary option. Capital One's transfer to Qatar takes 2–5 days, so you'll want to confirm availability first and ideally put the seat on a 24-hour hold if possible before initiating the transfer. Venture X and Venture card holders have access to this path.

Marriott Bonvoy® Points → Qatar Avios at 3:1 — This is the least efficient path. The 3:1 ratio means you're effectively diluting your Bonvoy points, and transfers take 1–5 days. Use this only as a top-off strategy if you're a few thousand Avios short and have Bonvoy points sitting idle.

Recent findings suggest that this is a huge deal that deserves its own callout. Qatar charges zero fuel surcharges on Qatar-operated award flights. This is not universal — British Airways Avios, for example, can pile on $700+ in carrier-imposed surcharges on longhaul awards. With Qatar Privilege Club, what you see is what you pay: 75,000 Avios plus the government taxes, which are typically modest.

Industry observers note that qatar allows stopovers in Doha and open-jaw routing on award tickets. This means you can build a trip that stops in Doha — giving you access to the Al Mourjan Business Lounge, one of the world's premier airport lounges — before continuing to a final destination. The stopover rule turns a single award redemption into a multi-destination experience, a classic FI travel rewards optimization move.

The key insight is that you are booking through BA's system using BA's pricing, but flying on Qatar's hardware — and Qatar's business class product is in a completely different league than BA's Club World. This mismatch between the booking partner's award chart and the operating airline's product quality is exactly what makes this a sweet spot.

The Triathlete editorial team has been around long enough that we’ve collectively written dozens of holiday gift guides — from stocking stuffers to price point round-ups to personality-based ideas, always solid ideas but usually pretty generic.

But this year, we wanted to get more personal and spread some holiday cheer along the way. So the editors made a list of some of our most consistent writers and hand-selected gifts to match each of them. We sent the gifts to their doors and hoped we’d hit the mark.

Sources indicate that and we are happy to share our IRL gift ideas with you for your own gifting or wish list creation. Below, you’ll find out a little bit more about some of our favorite contributors, what we gifted them, and why we think they’ll enjoy it.

It has been revealed that about the contributor: Sara is lucky enough to live in the triathlete’s dream training locale: Kailua-Kona, Hawaii, home of the Ironman World Championship. Though there’s lots to envy, I’m particularly green over her access to daily open-water swimming. But I also worry because swimming in open water comes with more risks than the typical pool.

What we gifted (and why): Sara’s frequent open-water swimming is why I’m gifting her this safety buoy from Tri-Fit. It’s bright, so she’s visible to other swimmers and from shore, and stable in the water if she needs to use it to adjust her goggles or shake off a calf cramp. But wait, there’s more! What I really love about this buoy is that it goes beyond your standard safety product – it’s an actual training workhorse, with a 1-liter hydration bladder and bite valve for days when Sara decides she wants to swim with the dolphins and sea turtles a little longer.

About the contributor: Sierra is a skilled writer who has lent her talents to highlight the need for more athlete-friendly pregnancy and postpartum deferral policies and to advocate for clearer policies around breastfeeding and pumping during races. She’s a mom to an active toddler.

What we gifted (and why): Life as a mom is busy and includes plenty of extras – like the armful of toys your child just has to bring with them to leave the house. As a fellow mom, I know what it feels like to not have enough arms to hold all the water bottles, snacks, and gear that comes with both triathlon and motherhood, so a bag with a pocket for everything can be a ready-made way of getting out of the house for training in an organized state, even when life as a mom feels far from organized.

—Rebekah Brately, associate editor.

About the contributor: Emma-Kate is a retired professional triathlete who’s still very much involved in the sport while continuing to multisport train and lift regularly. From her home in Boulder, Colorado, she interviews experts, talks to today’s top pro athletes, and writes to make changes and news of the sport understandable to all athletes.

What we gifted (and why): Winters in Colorado are long and cold, making training challenging. As a tri nerd, I think Emma-Kate will enjoy keeping up with her training indoors using the latest swim tech. While I don’t think ZWIM will keep her from the gym (I’m not sure anything could), I do think it will complement her training nicely to make the winter not feel so long.

Recent findings suggest that about the contributor: Tim is one of my favorite storytellers in triathlon, and I feel lucky to not only get to edit his stories regularly, but to hear the stories behind the stories. I can’t repeat most of them in print, but trust me when I say Tim Heming has seen some wild stuff.

What we gifted (and why): Naturally, when I read Mike Reilly’s book, Finding Your Finish Line, I thought of Tim. Reilly, also known as the “Voice of Ironman,” announced over 350,000 athletes across the finish line during his career as a race announcer before retiring in 2022. He, too, has seen it all, and some of his best tales are in this book. If I could get Tim and Mike in the same room to swap stories, it would probably be the best day of my triathlon career.

Sources indicate that reilly’s book, co-written with Triathlete contributor Sarah Wassner Flynn, is a masterful piece of storytelling. It’s inspirational, aspirational, and will leave you feeling proud to be a triathlete.

It has been revealed that about the contributor: Susan is a board-certified sports dietitian, accomplished Ironman athlete and Kona qualifier, and runs her own business helping endurance athletes dial in their health and performance goals through their nutrition. She is our go-to writer whenever we need a sports nutrition concept or topic broken down in a way that triathletes can apply to their own training and racing.

What we gifted (and why): I’ve been a long-time fan of Skratch Labs for its simple ingredients and clean flavors. When we saw Skratch now offers a make-it-yourself gel-making kit using its super high-carb sports drink mix, we thought the nutrition expert who literally wrote our guide on high-carb fueling might enjoy easily customizing her nutrition intake. More than the fueling customization, the kit also provides a less gooey gel texture and planet-friendly reusable soft flasks. I’m eager to hear how it works for her!

—Bethany Mavis, contributing editor.

About the contributor: When college student Saqib came on board as an intern in our Endurance department, the first question I had for this gangly cross-country runner was, “Have you done a triathlon?” The answer was no, and I am making it my life’s mission to change that.

I landed on the reasonably priced Valo Spark that had decent reviews.

Whether he loves it or uses it as a portable night light, I can’t wait to find out what he thinks!

Few people know the triathlon world better than Jordan, past or present. (She’s our first pick for a triathlon trivia team.) With her finger on the pulse, she gives pros and age-groupers a voice and digs into the stories shaping the sport.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Industry observers note that just the other day a friend getting into gravel was asking me about suspension parts for his relatively fresh gravel bike. He was considering different suspension components as a means to gain comfort while he rides—especially on chunkier gravel. He mentioned his frame isn’t compatible with a suspension fork, but was looking at parts like a suspension stem and suspension seatpost. If this sounds like you read this before hitting add to cart on those parts.

When I ran a shop I installed plenty of suspension parts on bikes for people who felt it was the only way they could be more comfortable on the bike. Certain riders fit the bill for a suspension seat post or suspension stem. A few customers had prostate complications and a suspension seat post helped them stay on the bike longer. Others had wrist or hand issues and they benefited from a suspension stem. But even those riders could get additional comfort from a simple change.

According to recent reports, after trying all the suspension components I could add to my own bike (as well as trying a full-suspension gravel bike), I have realized that throwing suspension at a gravel bike doesn’t necessarily fix the issue of being more comfortable on the ride. In the shop, customers would ask about installing a suspension fork on a hybrid or gravel bike, but not all frames are even compatible with a suspension fork.

Industry observers note that adding suspension parts to the bike can change the overall feel of the bike, not to mention the weight those parts typically add. When riders are looking for more comfort on their gravel bike the component swap I pick first is simple—wider tires. Here we’ll talk about the benefits of wider tires and why going tubeless gives your ride that extra bit of cush.

Step one of getting more comfortable on your gravel bike is setting up your tires as tubeless if they aren’t already set up that way. Tubeless systems allow you to run your pressure lower compared to running tubes, which in combination with a wider tire offers more comfort. Running tubes with a lower tire pressure leaves you susceptible to pinch flats, but tubeless systems remove the tubes from the equation.

According to recent reports, one easy way to check if your tires are set up as tubeless is to loosen the nut at the bottom of your valve and gently press it into the rim. If you press it in and air starts to come out, then tighten the nut back up—congratulations, your tires are set up as tubeless!

In a recent development, if they aren’t tubeless, then it’s time to check compatibility. Check the specs of your bike to see if your rim and tire are tubeless-compatible. If they aren’t you’ll have to explore latest wheel and tire options, but if they’re compatible you can convert them to tubeless. Some bikes come stock with tubeless-compatible rims and tires, but don’t come set up tubeless out of the box. Tubeless systems require specific rim tape or rim strips to properly set them up. I’ve seen plenty of bikes come with tubes installed, but with rims taped with tubeless tape. Again, check your individual bike’s specs to see if this includes your bike.

If you need to pull the tubes out of your tubeless-compatible wheels and tires, then you’ll need a few things. First is a good set of tubeless valves. My favorite are Muc-Off Tubeless Valves. They come with a valve core remover tool on the valve cap, come in different lengths depending on your rim depth, and there are a myriad of colors to add a little pop to your bike. You’ll also need tubeless sealant. I’ve tested more sealants than I can remember, but the tried-and-true sealant I go back to is Stan’s Sealant. Tara Seplavy, Bicycling’s Deputy Editor, walks through setting up your tubeless tires here.

According to recent reports, A bike rarely comes stock with the widest tire that fits in the bike. For example, the Trek Checkpoint SL5 is equipped with 700x42mm, but can fit up to 700x50mm tires when there are no fenders on the bike. Always check the technical specifications for your specific make and model to see how wide you can go. Over the last few years, bike manufacturers have been pushing the envelope to allow for wider and wider tires on bikes. If you have a previous model-year bike that doesn’t mean you can bank on the current model’s tire clearance fitting your bike. Be sure to check the correct generation for your specific make and model. If you go with a tire wider than the maximum width for your bike, you risk damaging the fork and frame.

On my own gravel rig, I recently bumped from 700x40mm tires to 700x45mm tires and noticed the difference immediately. I stuck with the same tire make and model—the Pirelli Cinturato H. The extra five millimeters of width immediately gave more comfort and traction on chunkier gravel and some local singletrack; even with the same tire tread. Five millimeters might not sound like a lot, but it added significant comfort while putting out rides longer than one hundred miles.

Sources indicate that wider tires are the right choice for many—even if you aren’t pushing your mileage into the triple digits. Recently I bumped up the tire width on my dad’s gravel bike. Adding wider tires to his bike (as well as a slightly thicker handlebar tape) leveled up his comfort level while riding. Whether you are taking your gravel bike on singletrack, chunky gravel, hundred-mile rides, or just want a little more comfort on your local lunch loop, go tubeless and bump up your tire width.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

#114212. How to Find Stability and Freedom in Supported Headstand

How to Find Stability and Freedom in Supported Headstand

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2562 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yogajournal

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that in Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past complications beginning in 1975.
  • It has been revealed that “Sthera sukham asanam,” “Posture is steady and comfortable,” notes Patanjali in the first of his three sutras on asana.
  • Because balancing in Headstand (Sirsasana) is such a challenge, it forces us to look deeply into our posture and our nervous system to discover an inner sense of balance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past complications beginning in 1975. This article about Headstand first appeared in the July-August 1990 matter of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

It has been revealed that “Sthera sukham asanam,” “Posture is steady and comfortable,” notes Patanjali in the first of his three sutras on asana. But as even experienced yoga students know, “steady and comfortable” are not the first words that come to mind to describe the sensation of standing on one’s head. And many couch potatoes would probably insist that they feel quite steady and comfortable as they sprawl out in front of the tube. So what exactly does Patanjali mean by the words sthira and sukham?

Because balancing in Headstand (Sirsasana) is such a challenge, it forces us to look deeply into our posture and our nervous system to discover an inner sense of balance. This interiorization of awareness can reveal some of the subtleties behind Patanjali’s words.

According to recent reports, the word thira comes from the Sanskrit root tha, meaning “to stand,” which is also the root of the English words “stay,” “stable,” and “steady.” This root verb is of great importance in the Yoga Sutras. Patanjali first uses it in defining the term abhyasa, or practice, in Sutra I-13: “Practice is the endeavor toward stillness and stability of the mindfield.” According to Pandit Usharbhud Arya’s commentary, “Meditation means bringing the mind to stillness or stability, which means freedom from the rajasic and tamasic turbulences, the mind’s one-pointed concentration on a single sattic vrtti harmonious vibration remaining uninterrupted so that the mind flows in a calm, pacific, smooth stream.”.

For a hatha yoga practitioner, the following question arises: How can I bring this level of mental stillness into an asana such as Headstand, and, conversely, how can I adjust in the asana to stabilize and deepen the mental stillness? In other words, how can I explore the states of thira and sukham in the pose?

Recent findings suggest that in previous asana columns, we have looked at the relationship of the bones, the flesh, and the skin to posture, circulation, and breathing. We have seen that the muscle fibers assist in circulation through their pumping action and that when they are open to the free flow of the breath, they can subtly communicate with the inner lining of the skin. Stability and comfort are accompanied by stable, grounded bones, effortless breathing, a fluid feeling of the flesh, and a sensitive inner skin. Fear, insecurity, and instability, on the other hand, are accompanied by hardened muscles, disturbed breathing, restricted blood flow, collapsed joints, and insensitive skin. The question now becomes: How can I organize the bones, muscle fibers, and skin to create a stable posture that allows the breath and bodily fluids to flow freely?

According to recent reports, freedom or restriction of the breath and bodily fluids can be experienced in the expansion, contraction, and inner pressure of the body’s three main cavities: the pelvic-abdominal cavity (from the diaphragm to the pelvic floor), the thoracic cavity, and the skull. In any posture, the respiratory rhythm begins with an expansion of the thoracic cavity, accomplished by the contraction and descent of the diaphragm and the lifting and widening of the rib cage by the intercostal and other respiratory muscles. This expansion creates a negative pressure (lower than normal atmospheric pres sure) in the chest, drawing air from outside the body into the lungs. With the exhalation, a positive pressure (higher than normal atmospheric pressure) is created as the expansion ceases and the elastic recoil of the lung tissue presses the air out of the lungs.

In soft, quiet breathing, there is no resistance to this cycle. The pelvic-abdominal cavity expands and releases in harmony with the thoracic cavity, and air flows in and out of the body without impedence. The expansion and contraction of the body is perfectly matched by the movement of air in and out of the lungs. Because of this balance, the sensation of interior pressure remains constant throughout the body.

However, any unnecessary tension in the body will create resistance to the breath and a corresponding increase in resistance to the circulatory fluids. This resistance creates the sensation of increased internal pressure, a sensation to which the brain and skull are especially sensitive. To experience this sensation in an exaggerated way, inhale, close your mouth, close your nostrils with your fingers, and try to exhale.

It has been revealed that notice the immediate increase in pressure in the brain. Close your mouth and nostrils after exhaling and you will experience a slightly different pressure increase.

Tension anywhere in the body will have a similar pressurizing effect. For example, neck and shoulder tension restricts the expansion of the rib cage, disrupting the respiratory rhythm and increasing the pressure in the skull. Psychological stresses tend to be reflected in a tense diaphragm, and the diaphragm also reacts to tension in the groins and pelvic region. When the groins are open, the bones of the legs, pelvis, and lower spine support the weight of the body, and the muscles of that region are free to expand and contract with the breathing cycle. However, when the groins are restricted, the pelvic floor cannot.

Recent findings suggest that “breathe,” and this resistance in the pelvic-abdominal region impedes the movement of the diaphragm. This constriction of the breath creates pressure in the skull, just as you experienced when you held your mouth and nostrils shut.

According to recent reports, standing on one’s head exacerbates all of these restrictions to the breath. The shoulders and neck are often tensed to hold on to the body. Fears of falling tighten the diaphragm. The legs and pelvis are often collapsed and unconscious. Thus the breath will be constricted and the brain will feel pressurized. The most obvious aspect of this syndrome is that blood cannot move out of the skull, leading to a sense of congestion. (Some degree of pressure is usual when first starting to practice Headstand; a beginner should not expect to feel perfectly quiet and comfortable right away. But if the eyes become bloodshot or if extreme pressure is felt in the eyes or ears, the pose is being done incorrectly and should not be held. Seek guidance from a qualified teacher.).

It has been revealed that the increased pressure in the skull results from a breakdown in the pumping system of the body. The diaphragm is a large pump for moving air, and the skeletal muscles must pump fluids back to the heart to maintain circulation. To facilitate these processes of circulation and respiration, the body is organized into six regions, each with its own “relay station” to oversee the movement of fluids and breath in and out of that region. Although most of these relay stations do not have a single specialized physical component like the diaphragmatic muscle, I will refer to them as diaphragms for lack of a better term, because, like the diaphragm, they function as pumps. (The term “diaphragm” is a convenient metaphor for the complex set of physiological and psychological mechanisms that control the movement of fluids, air, and energy in and out of a particular area of the body.

These diaphragms and their powerful effects can be experienced subjectively by turning the attention inward, although most of them cannot be objectively revealed through dissection.) These diaphragmatic regions, as introduced to me by my teacher, Ramanand Patel, are the brain, the throat, the heart, the respiratory diaphragm, the navel, and the pelvic floor.

In order to attain thira and sukham in Headstand, all six diaphragms must be functioning properly. However, this article will focus on the first and sixth diaphragm, as these are particularly important.

In a recent development, the sixth diaphragm has a tangible physical component, the muscles of the pelvic floor. Open groins, strong legs, and stable hip joints are necessary for the healthy functioning of this diaphragm, which should move synchronously with the physical diaphragm, creating the sense that the pelvis and abdomen breathe freely:.

It has been revealed that correct action of the pelvic diaphragm stabilizes the coccyx bone and helps circulate fluids in and out of the legs. Its location is the first chakra, the chakra of grounding and stability, and thus it plays an important role in developing the quality of shira.

The first diaphragm is the brain or skull diaphragm, responsible for moving energy in the form of blood and cerebrospinal fluid) in and out of the brain. This diaphragm has no muscular components; rather, it is composed of a complex combination of neural pathways and blood vessels. My experience has been that it moves in opposition to the other five diaphragms: When the other five diaphragms are “inhaling,” or drawing energy in, the brain diaphragm is “exhaling,” or releasing. Conversely, when the lower five are exhaling, the brain “inhales.” This is the rhythm that accompanies a healthy nervous and circulatory system, leading to shira and sukham.

However, if the pelvic diaphragm is locked or inhibited, the brain diaphragm will “inhale” along with the torso, leading to an increase in tension in the muscles and pressure in the skull. This tension can also be felt as disturbances in the skin, eyes, ears, and tongue.

Before attempting Headstand, you should have a strong, stable Downward-Facing Dog Pose and a regular standing pose practice to ensure the strength, flexibility, and intelligence of your arms and legs necessary to protect the neck and skull. Use a firm blanket or mat for the head. If possible, learn to balance in a corner of the room, resting one foot on each wall to prevent tilting to one side or another. If a corner is not available, use any wall, placing your hands close to the wall to keep from arching your back into a banana shape.

Place your forearms on the floor, interlocking your fingers evenly and completely and keeping your wrists perpendicular to the floor. Your elbows should be exactly shoulder width apart. This foundation must be stabilized by constant practice.

In building this foundation, several difficulties may be encountered. One arm may overpower the other, distorting the shoulders, forearms, and wrists and torquing the foundation. Learn to press evenly into both arms. Your wrists may collapse outward, losing their grounding and strength. Consciously hold the thumb side of your wrists toward each other. Your elbows may splay apart. Maintain a constant pressure from your outer elbows toward each other, as if your elbows were pressing into a block held between them. However, do not draw them closer than shoulder width.

Having established this stable foundation, place your head up against your wrists and palms, cupping your skull without losing the strength of the wrists. Taking the weight onto the arms and not the neck, use the strength of the groins and pelvis to lift both legs up from the floor. (Beginners will probably have to throw one leg up at a time, but as soon as possible should begin lifting both at once.) Resting your feet against the wall, lift the weight of the body out of the shoulders, away from the neck.

Learning this lifting action is more vital than learning to balance. Only when the lift is strong and the balance stable should you move to the center of the room.

In a recent development, students who can balance steadily in the center of the room can begin to explore the effect on the pose of the pelvic and brain diaphragms. Most beginning students look something like the “inverted banana” in Figure 1. Your shoulders sink, the floating ribs and upper lumbar hang forward, your back body collapses, and your legs fall behind the midline. With no vertical extension, the weight of the torso collapses onto your neck and skull, compressing the brain diaphragm. The legs are not lifting, and their weight hardens the posterior pelvic floor and the inner front groins. The anterior coccyx bone hangs unsupported.

According to recent reports, instead, your arms and shoulders must lift actively away from the neck and skull. Figure 2 demonstrates a close-up of the correct lifting action. Note the widening of the upper inner shoulder blades and the lifting of the inner and outer deltoid muscles, which lifts the weight of the torso away from the neck and skull. This action can be learned in Downward-Facing Dog (Adho Mukha Svanasana).

Industry observers note that your legs also must be brought forward, lifting the lumbar, pelvis, and legs to eliminate the banana-like collapse. Intermediate students often learn this action, only to close the anterior pelvis and inner groins and lose the support of the posterior coccyx (see Figure 3). The front and inner groins must be dynamically extended, without collapsing onto the lumbar. Your legs must work tremendously in Headstand to open the pelvic diaphragm. In working the legs, be sure to extend the bones from the pelvis without hardening and tensing the muscles—rather, keep the muscles vibrant. If the leg muscles harden, the pelvic diaphragm will tighten and the brain will become pressurized and confused.

Industry observers note that in the completed position (Figure 5), your front body and back body extend evenly, aligning the bones with gravity. When the bones are aligned, they can support the weight of the body without muscular strain. Figure 4 has been inverted to show the alignment of the arches, knees, hips, shoulders, and ears. By lifting evenly out of the pelvis, the bones of the legs free the pelvic diaphragm to breathe and pump blood to the legs. The dynamic action of the legs lifts the weight of the torso from the skull, allowing the brain diaphragm to breathe.

Sources indicate that the anterior and posterior sides of the coccyx bone are supported, freeing the pelvic diaphragm. This freedom allows the respiratory diaphragm to breathe easily, which in turn allows the brain to feel relaxed and spacious. Thus the whole pose feels spacious, stable, and comfortable.

In a recent development, stability and comfort are prerequisites for deeper work in the poses. As Vyassa says in his commentary to the first of the Yoga Sutras, yoga is samadhi. Sthira and sukham are the beginning of the samadhi state and thus are the point at which true yoga commences. All previous action is preparatory in nature. To achieve thira and sukham, it is not sufficient just to sit in any comfortable pose. Rather, you must perfect the pose to such an extent that samadhi can spontaneously awaken.

It has been revealed that the universe is alive, awakening and creating itself anew with each moment. If we create the proper foundations of shira and sukham, so that our mind and body are clear and calm, we can directly experience this awakening and creativity. With 10 years until the turn of the millenium, human consciousness is awakening to its own inner potentials as it is simultaneously awakening to the potentials of the natural world. All serious practitioners of yoga should work to be stabilized at least in the beginning level of thira and sukham by then, so we can usher in a new age of planetary awakening, with wisdom, compassion, and ecological communion with the natural world as our goals.

#114211. Clipless Pedals Can Feel Intimidating—Here Are Some Tips to Make Those First Clipless Rides Feel Smoother

📅 07 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1726 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bicycling ↗ Open Full Page

Clipless Pedals Can Feel Intimidating—Here Are Some Tips to Make Those First Clipless Rides Feel Smoother

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1726 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that when a rider switches from flat pedals to clipless pedals, they typically aren’t thinking about the differences of pedals like Shimano SPD or SPD-SL, Wahoo Speedplays, or egg-beater pedals.
  • Industry observers note that not all people considering the switch realize this—as contradictory as it sounds, clipless pedals refer to a pedal system where you are clipped into the pedal.
  • Here we’ll dig into what clipless pedals are, how they can benefit you on your ride, tips for setting up your pedals and cleats, and tips for those daunting first few rides with your new pedals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when a rider switches from flat pedals to clipless pedals, they typically aren’t thinking about the differences of pedals like Shimano SPD or SPD-SL, Wahoo Speedplays, or egg-beater pedals. Many times, they haven’t heard of Time pedals or the different Assioma or Garmin models. The first thought many have is, “How do I get out of the pedal once I’m clipped in?”.

Industry observers note that not all people considering the switch realize this—as contradictory as it sounds, clipless pedals refer to a pedal system where you are clipped into the pedal. If you aren’t familiar with the system, think about being clipped into a ski binding. Some pedal options offer different release settings—similar to how a DIN setting on a ski binding can be adjusted to offer different levels of force needed to release the ski boot from the binding.

Here we’ll dig into what clipless pedals are, how they can benefit you on your ride, tips for setting up your pedals and cleats, and tips for those daunting first few rides with your new pedals.

I have plenty of friends who swear by the saying, “flat pedals win medals.” However, there is a reason you’ll only see clipless pedals at world tour road races or on the majority of gravel bikes at your local gravel grinder. When you ride clipped in you end up using more of your leg musculature during each revolution of your pedal stroke.

It has been revealed that in short, this means you’re typically more efficient when using clipless pedals compared to flat pedals. For clarity, you don’t need to ride clipless pedals to be a cyclist. But for those riders looking to take their riding to the next level, it’s worth giving them a try.

Because you’re literally attached to the pedal, you use not only your quads in the downstroke part of the revolution, but you also work your hamstrings, hip flexors, and glutes as you pull up. All of those muscles at work translate to more power while you’re riding, especially as you refine your pedaling technique. To get started, here’s your expert-backed guide to pedaling with clipless pedals—without falling over.

“Cleat placement is paramount,” says Issac Denham, owner of bike fitting studio Befitting Bicycles in Wayne, Pennsylvania. “Since incorrect cleat placement can lead to injuries, we suggest booking time with a bike fitter to place your cleats. Having a professional install your cleats also ensures that they won’t be installed improperly or even upside down.”.

For those riders that want to try clipless pedals, but don’t want to jump into a precision fit, start with cleats in a neutral position. This means setting the cleats up in the middle of the slots in the shoe with the cleats relatively straight. Just make sure the left and right cleats are in roughly the same position—this will give you a good baseline moving forward.

It will take time doing the guess and check method for cleat placement, but this method gives you the chance to play around going clipless before you invest hundreds into a bike fit. If you start to develop pain after using clipless pedals, stop pedaling. This is likely due to cleat position and that is when it is time to see a local trusted shop for direction.

“Many clipless pedals have adjustable pedal tension. This is basically how hard the built-in spring holds the cleat in the pedal,” says Dan Chabonov, Bicycling test editor. “Setting this tension as low as possible means you need less force to clip in and out of the pedals and can make the learning process a little easier.”.

While most clipless pedals already come set at the lowest tension setting from the manufacturer, you can also easily make the adjustment.

Industry observers note that “Typically out of the box, pedals are set up with the least amount of release tension,” notes Becky Quinn, former pro and bike fitter. “The pedal tensioner is on the rear of the pedal. There is a small 3mm bolt that requires a 3mm Allen wrench to adjust the tension. It can be turned counterclockwise to loosen the tension or clockwise to tighten it. There is a small window on the back of the pedal that has a small horizontal pin that moves up or down depending on which way you turn the tensioner.”.

If you adjust the tension on your pedals, make sure you confirm that the pins are in the same place on both the left and right pedal, so the release tension is the same on both sides.

Practice does indeed make perfect when it comes to learning how to pedal with clipless pedals. The goal is to become so comfortable with the movements that they become part of your muscle memory, so you don’t have to look down at your foot or pedal for longer than a quick glance.

When you’re just starting out pedaling with clipless pedals, do it inside first. “Practicing indoors either on a trainer, or even leaned up against a wall, can be a great place to start where you don’t have to worry about falling down or looking silly,” says Denham.

Industry observers note that when I ran a shop and was getting people set up on clipless pedals, I would suggest they get on the bike inside, ideally on a trainer or next to a wall to stabilize themselves, then put on a show or a movie. It sounds monotonous (and the people you live with might give you an odd look or two), but simply clip in, clip out, clip in, clip out, over and over. Do it looking down at your shoe, then when that’s comfortable practice doing it without looking down. Feel it out inside and you’ll be much better off when you head out the door.

To clip into your pedal, start with the pedal positioned at the bottom of the pedal stroke.

Industry observers note that “Softly lift the front of the pedal with your toe to flip it over so that you can engage. Your toe will be slightly pointed downward. Slide your foot forward until the tongue of the cleat stops on the lip of the pedal,” Quinn explains. “Once you can’t slide your foot any further forward, continue to pedal forward and add pressure to the pedal. It will click in. Sometimes you will need to rotate your heel inward or outward at the 6 o’clock position to engage securely.”.

Then it’s time to clip out: “In order to practice clipping out of your pedals, place one leg all the way down to the bottom of the pedal stroke (6 o’clock). Then, firmly rotate your heel outward. Be sure to not roll your ankle,” Quinn advises. “The motion should be similar to that of smashing a bug under the ball of your foot.”.

If there is a single gem of advice we would love to pass on to every cyclist who has ever learned how to ride with clipless pedals, this would be it: Unclip the foot you intend to put down when you come to a stop before you come to a stop. “This is the most important piece of the puzzle,” notes Quinn.

Sources indicate that once you unclip, “here is the most critical piece: Keep the unclipped foot on the pedal but continue to pedal a half stroke,” Quinn adds. “Once the foot that is still clipped in gets to the 6 o’clock position, coast and stand up. Your butt needs to get off the saddle. Continue to apply your rear brakes until you are almost at a stop. When you are about to come to a complete stop, apply your front brake and step down with the unclipped foot.”.

Many cleat and pedal systems will follow a similar process with the general idea being: line up the cleat on the pedal and add downward force to clip in once the cleat is aligned.

It has been revealed that remember how we said switching to clipless pedals is a cycling rite of passage of sorts? Well, so is falling over as you’re learning. Practicing while riding on grass can make the falls a little easier, and falling with the proper technique (yes, there’s a technique for falling, too!) will lower your chances of serious injury.

“You will fall. We all have done it and it’s okay,” notes Quinn. “Just remember that if you start to fall over, turn your buttocks so you land on it. It is the most padding we have on our bodies. Putting out an arm can break a wrist. You most likely will only get a bruise on your butt.”.

It has been revealed that the most notable thing is not to get in your head, beat yourself up, or give up. Falling over at least a few times has happened to every single cyclist who rides with clipless pedals.

I’ll never forget one of my first rides with clipless pedals. I rolled over to the group in the parking lot overly confident, forgot I had to unclip my foot from the pedal, and slowly tipped over—still attached to the bike. It happens to everyone when you’re first making the switch, but some practice at home can make the transition a little less painful.

Natascha Grief is the fitness and reviews editor for Women’s Health. She writes about fitness, health, performance, everyday movement, and the products that help people train and recover better. She brings more than a decade of experience as a NASM-certified personal trainer focused on training women, with specialties in functional strength training, corrective exercise, nutrition, and behavior change. She previously worked as the health and fitness editor at Bicycling, and her writing has appeared in Runner’s World and other outlets. Across her work, she’s especially focused on making complex wellness, training, and performance topics approachable and accessible.

It has been revealed that jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

#114210. Breaking: What’s the Minimum Amount of Mileage You Can Do to Maintain Fitness? Experts Answer

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1370 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Runnersworld ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: What’s the Minimum Amount of Mileage You Can Do to Maintain Fitness? Experts Answer

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1370 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For some runners, taking a week or two off from running after a race is the hard part—they can’t wait to ramp back up their volume again.
  • Sources indicate that still, if you trained for months to build up the fitness, including your aerobic capacity, lactate threshold, and running economy, you probably want to try to maintain at least some of that afterward.
  • Maintenance mode also gives you the flexibility to be able to jump into a 10K or half-marathon on a whim, claims Mike Sheehy, running coach for Team Abbott who has completed more than 100 marathons.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For some runners, taking a week or two off from running after a race is the hard part—they can’t wait to ramp back up their volume again. But for others, crossing a finish line (of any distance) might feel like a natural point to take a break from the sport, or at least to significantly scale back.

Sources indicate that still, if you trained for months to build up the fitness, including your aerobic capacity, lactate threshold, and running economy, you probably want to try to maintain at least some of that afterward. That way, you can go into a spring training cycle with a solid base.

Maintenance mode also gives you the flexibility to be able to jump into a 10K or half-marathon on a whim, claims Mike Sheehy, running coach for Team Abbott who has completed more than 100 marathons.

According to recent reports, keeping a steady mileage base also allows you to experiment. “This gives you a chance to try latest fuels, try new gear, a new pair of shorts, new pair of shoes, stuff you didn't like during your block,” Sheehy indicates. You could also experiment with pace. “This is a great block to think about moving your easy pace up 15 seconds to let your heart and body start adapting to that new norm.”.

It has been revealed that if you want to strike a balance between giving yourself a well-deserved break and completely reversing all of your gains, the question becomes: What’s the minimum running you can do to maintain your fitness? And how long can I do that without falling back?

Here’s what running coaches and an exercise physiologist have to say, plus what other forms of exercise come into play in the maintenance phase.

GET YOUR MAINTENANCE INTENDS HERE.

First, it’s important to note that taking a week or two off after a marathon and at least one week for the half is not only encouraged, it’s probably the best thing you can do for your body—and your mind.

“The thing I encourage all my runners to remember is patience,” claims Sheehy. “Let your body heal and take that time.” He typically advises runners to take a full week off, then slowly add in easy miles without rushing to get back to quality workouts.

Then by the end of week two, you enter the true maintenance phase. “This is really an exciting time of running,” Sheehy states. “This is where we’re keeping 90 percent of the fitness with about 60 percent of the work.” He recommends taking the average mileage from your peak marathon training weeks rather than the single highest weekly mileage.

This tends to net out to between 20 and 30 miles a week in the maintenance phase for marathon runners and 10 to 15 miles a week for half-marathoners. That might look like three shorter, easier runs during the week and an 8- to 12-miler on the weekend. (Experts agree it’s best to run more frequently at lower volume for each run than do fewer, longer runs.) “That keeps you 90 percent fit, but allows you to enjoy running and not have the pressure of having to run six or five days a week and without having structured workouts,” Sheehy indicates.

Sources indicate that andrew M. Jones, Ph.D., professor of applied physiology at the University of Exeter in the U.K., puts the minimum effective dose of maintenance running slightly lower—at 50 percent—though after about four to six weeks at half the volume, runners will likely start to see “more significant deterioration,” he indicates, specifically of race-specific endurance. (Running economy may be more resilient.).

That’s not necessarily a bad thing (and allows you to focus on other goals; more on this soon), and 50 percent is enough to preserve a foundation to allow you to pick up at the beginning of a 16-week marathon training plan with relative ease.

Greg Laraia, a running coach at Motiv in New York City, agrees and provides this example: Say a runner finished Berlin on September 27 and plans to run London on April 24. After time off, he’d have them work back up to 50 percent of their mileage by October 25, then hover in the 50 to 60 percent of mileage range until early January when their London block would start in earnest.

Retaining intensity during the maintenance phase is arguably more crucial than frequency and duration, per Jones. “It’s impossible to give a minimum effective dose [for intensity] but ideally by week two [after a marathon] they’d get back to the pre-marathon training intensity but with lower volume,” he states, which might be lower duration and/or frequency of quality running. “Intensity is the key stimulus.”.

To hit this stimulus, Sheehy and Laraia both like to have runners add in strides (e.g., four to six 30- to 60-second strides as part of an easy run) before doing more intense speed workouts that could make their way back into the weekly schedule about a month after a race.

Sheehy provides an example of a speed workout he likes to include during the maintenance phase:.

Industry observers note that “The latest race pace is something I know they can achieve that is apparent in previous race results and workouts; not some aspirational wish pace,” Sheehy indicates. “This will give them the confidence they need or maybe a wake up call, but it makes for a great starting point, and allows us to calibrate their easy paces and use the lower volumes to let their body (and heart) adjust to the new norm.”.

It has been revealed that sheehy cautions against swapping out runs that make up your maintenance mileage for other cardio, as it is notable to maintain the specificity of running if you want to maintain running fitness. But he often adds in an indoor cycling day during his offseason on top of four or so days of running. If you dropped down your running frequency, an aerobic cross-training workout can support your fitness maintenance. Plus, it gives you a mental break, Jones claims.

It has been revealed that laraia notes one case where swapping maintenance miles for other cardio could make sense would be when runners come off a fall race injured or worn down and simply need a break from running so much. “Running is always going to be the best option because running is the sport, but if an elliptical or a bike is going to make you miss [running] enough to want to do it again, let’s start there,” he says.

The maintenance phase is also a great time to focus on strength training, Jones notes. Sheehy agrees, suggesting aiming for two to three days a week. You can do more volume (either via an extra day or more sets/reps) during this phase, but it’s still notable to include one true rest day in your blueprint, Sheehy says.

Recent findings suggest that strength work helps to build neuromuscular capacity, improve power that can translate to speed, and strengthen your tendons and ligaments for the upcoming season, especially if you focus on heavier lifting. “Let’s get comfortable with the extra load and then let’s see if it makes running better and more efficient,” Laraia says.

GET YOUR STRENGTH WORKOUTS HERE.

Laraia claims signs that you may have pulled back too much include a higher-than-usual heart rate during runs or paces that feel harder than normal.

Industry observers note that still, it’s probably better to lose a little bit more running fitness in the offseason than to push yourself too hard, he claims. The former is going to put you in a better position to start a newly introduced training block in the spring, compared with the latter, which could lead to burnout and could set your next training cycle back.

Industry observers note that “Realistically, you’re going to be better off taking the extra day versus trying to push through something if you’re early in a block or just trying to maintain fitness,” Laraia states. “I’d rather you be 100 percent recovered for every run versus in the build,” where it might make sense to go into a run feeling a little depleted.
